terminal_record.title: AAPD Warned Project 2025 Could Threaten Disability Supports
terminal_record.description_short: AAPD said Project 2025 Medicaid funding and home-care proposals could threaten supports used by people with disabilities.
terminal_record.description_medium: On October 29, 2024, the American Association of People with Disabilities described Project 2025 proposals to shift Medicaid to block-grant or per-capita funding and to limit home- and community-based services. AAPD warned that the proposals could constrain services used by disabled people. This is an attributed warning about proposed policy; the source does not establish later enactment or implementation.
terminal_record.description_long: On October 29, 2024, the American Association of People with Disabilities (AAPD) published a policy brief about Project 2025 and its potential effects on disabled people. In its Medicaid section, AAPD said the plan sought to shift Medicaid toward block-grant or per-capita funding, and proposed narrowing access to home- and community-based services (HCBS). The brief explains that many disabled people rely on Medicaid-funded HCBS to live independently. AAPD warned that restricting Medicaid funding and HCBS eligibility could limit supports for people with disabilities. The warning describes projected consequences if proposals were adopted, not completed government actions. The supplied materials do not establish that the Trump administration abolished ADA accommodations or enforcement, enacted the Medicaid cuts in the prior description, caused a specific number of coverage losses, or forced people into institutions. They also do not show which, if any, of the proposals later became policy. This entry is therefore narrowed to AAPD's attributed 2024 warning about a policy blueprint, without presenting forecasts as realized harm or attributing the blueprint's proposals to a specific administration action.

The reporting contradicts this entry’s original claim that Trump called Williams ugly, a bad person, or bad at golf. This corrected record describes the supported event: Trump’s defense of Williams in response to criticism following the 2009 match. The source accounts do not establish the exact publication date of the original Trump University blog post or the number of people who read it. The frozen August date is also incorrect for the U.S. Open incident, which took place in September 2009.

terminal_record.title: Trump Uses “Animals” Remark During California Immigration Roundtable
terminal_record.description_short: Trump Used “Animals” Remark During May 2018 California Immigration Roundtable
terminal_record.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018, White House roundtable on sanctuary-city policies, President Donald Trump said, “These aren’t people. These are animals” after Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member she could not report to ICE. Trump’s reply referred broadly to “people coming into the country” without naming a group. The White House and Trump later said he meant MS-13; FactCheck.org said the original remark’s intended target could not be established with certainty.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 16, 2018, President Donald Trump held a White House roundtable with California mayors, sheriffs and other officials about sanctuary-city policies. During the discussion, Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member but could not tell ICE unless that person met a threshold. Trump replied that “people coming into the country” were “animals,” saying, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” In the official transcript, the remark immediately follows Mims’s reference to MS-13, but Trump’s reply does not name the gang. The White House press secretary later said Trump was referring to MS-13 gang members, and Trump said the next day that he meant MS-13. FactCheck.org reported those explanations while noting that it could not determine exactly what Trump meant in the original remark. The record should therefore describe the words and their immediate setting, then attribute the later clarification separately. It should not say the transcript proves that Trump was referring to all immigrants, or that it definitively proves he meant only MS-13. The sources establish the public remark and context; they do not document a resulting policy change or quantify harm caused by it.

children.title: Federal Agencies Cancel About $400 Million in Columbia Grants and Contracts
children.description_short: On March 7, 2025, federal agencies announced cancellation of about $400 million in grants and contracts to Columbia University.
children.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, four federal agencies announced the immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in grants and contracts to Columbia University. The Justice Department called it an initial round and tied the action to alleged failures to address harassment of Jewish students. Reuters reported that the government did not specify the affected grants or its evidence. This was a Columbia action, not a blanket three-university cutoff.
children.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the Departments of Justice, Health and Human Services, Education, and the General Services Administration announced the immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University. The Justice Department said it was the first round of action and tied the cancellations to what the administration described as Columbia’s inaction over harassment of Jewish students. Reuters reported that the administration did not identify which grants or contracts were affected or disclose its evidence for the stated rationale. This card describes a specific action against Columbia; it does not claim that every federal research or education dollar to the university ended. The sources also do not show a simultaneous action against Harvard and Yale. The supplied parent entry placed Columbia in an August 2025 three-university cutoff, but the documented Columbia action occurred in March and is distinct from the later Harvard action. The administration’s stated justification is attributed here, not presented as a judicial finding.

children.description_long: On April 14, 2025, Harvard rejected administration demands and the Trump administration announced a freeze on $2.2 billion in multi-year grants plus $60 million in multi-year contract value. The Department of Education described the action as a freeze; Reuters reported that it came within hours of Harvard’s rejection and said the university viewed the demands as ceding control and threatening academic freedom. This card concerns the announced action against Harvard alone. It does not show that every federal research and education fund was ended, that Yale was included, or that a simultaneous August action occurred. The administration attributed its decision to civil-rights concerns and campus antisemitism; those are its stated rationales, not independent findings established by these sources. The official announcement specifies multi-year grant and contract value, not all current or future federal money. The parent entry merged this April event with Columbia’s separate March cancellations and claimed a broader three-university cutoff.

terminal_record.title: DOJ Narrows One Proposed Google Antitrust Remedy While Continuing the Case
terminal_record.description_short: DOJ dropped its proposed requirement for Google to divest AI investments while continuing to seek Chrome divestiture in its search case.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department revised its proposed remedy in the Google search-monopoly case. Reuters reported that DOJ no longer sought mandatory divestiture of Google’s AI investments, instead seeking advance notice of future generative-AI investments. DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued to seek Chrome divestiture and other measures. The filing changed one proposed remedy; it did not end the case or establish a final court outcome.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposal in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. Reuters reported that DOJ dropped its proposed requirement that Google sell its investments in artificial-intelligence companies, including Anthropic, and shifted to requiring advance notice of future investments in generative AI. The same report said DOJ and 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Google to divest its Chrome browser and take other measures addressing the search monopoly a judge had found. This was a change to proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case. The filing left major remedies in dispute; it did not establish that any remedy had taken effect or that DOJ abandoned the action as a whole. The source describes a formal litigation proposal and attributes it to court papers filed in Washington. The supplied packet’s claim that the department dropped the case, or did so in exchange for donations, is not supported by this evidence and is omitted. Timing and campaign donations do not establish motive. The court’s final remedy and the case’s later disposition are outside the verified facts in this card.

terminal_record.title: Judge Halts CFPB Mass Firings After 1,400–1,500 Workers Are Dismissed
terminal_record.description_short: A federal judge suspended CFPB mass dismissals after 1,400–1,500 workers were fired.
terminal_record.description_medium: On April 17, 2025, the CFPB fired between 1,400 and 1,500 workers. The next day, a federal judge suspended those mass dismissals while considering whether the administration had violated an existing court order. Reuters reported concern about compliance but no final finding that the government had violated the injunction.
terminal_record.description_long:
On Thursday, April 17, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau fired between 1,400 and 1,500 workers, Reuters reported the following day. The dismissals would have eliminated as much as 90% of the agency’s workforce, according to the report. On April 18, U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson suspended the mass dismissals pending a decision about compliance with her prior injunction. Reuters reported that Jackson was deeply concerned about whether the agency was complying with the order; the article does not say she had reached a final violation finding.

The article also included a sworn declaration from an attorney representing an employee union that several CFPB offices, including ones responsible for supervision and consumer complaints, had lost all or all but one staff member. CFPB chief legal officer Mark Paoletta separately said the agency had followed court orders and assessed staffing needs. The competing statements matter: this card records the reported firings and the court’s immediate suspension while preserving that compliance was disputed. It does not claim the CFPB was legally disbanded or that every enforcement matter ended.

source_fact_map.quote: On Thursday, the agency fired between 1,400 and 1,500 workers, eliminating as much as 90% of its workforce.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
WASHINGTON, April 18 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Friday halted the mass firings carried out on Thursday afternoon at the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, saying she was deeply concerned the Trump administration had violated court orders setting conditions on dismissals.

On Thursday, the agency fired between 1,400 and 1,500 workers, eliminating as much as 90% of its workforce.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up here.

A witness statement filed on Friday morning also accused senior officials and an administration official associated with billionaire Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency of disregarding the court's orders. The witness said the DOGE member Gavin Kliger also demanded staff work a 36-hour shift without breaks and verbally abused staff. However, the Office of Personnel Management rejected the allegations as "an outright lie," asserting Kliger had not overseen the workforce reduction.

An appeals court last week ordered that firings at the CFPB could only occur after a "particularized assessment."

Mark Paoletta, the CFPB's chief legal officer, said in a sworn statement the agency had followed court orders and had conducted a detailed assessment of staffing needs. This evaluation found the agency's resources significantly exceeded both its needs and legal authorities, he said.

However, in a sworn declaration, Jennifer Bennett, an attorney representing an employee union, said offices across the CFPB - including critical, legally required functions such as supervision, consumer complaints, and military service member affairs - had either had all or all but one person terminated.

President Donald Trump and Musk have called to abolish the agency, accusing it without providing evidence of politicized enforcement and waste, but administration officials have said in court the CFPB will persist in some form.

"I am deeply concerned given the scope and speed of the agency's action ... about whether the agency is now in compliance with the preliminary injunction," U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson said during a hearing called after Thursday's dismissals.

Jackson ordered that Thursday's mass dismissals be suspended pending a decision on whether the government is in violation of her order. She said CFPB employees would not lose access to computer systems on Friday evening, as agency leadership had told them in Thursday's notices of dismissal.

terminal_record.description_long: This corrected entry records a February 2025 change in senior U.S. military leadership. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown on February 21 and described five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the same shake-up. The Associated Press reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth followed Brown’s dismissal by firing Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti, then chief of naval operations, and Air Force Gen. James Slife, vice chief of the Air Force; AP also reported on changes to the services’ top military lawyers. The supplied record asserted that officers were removed because they testified against Trump in impeachment proceedings. The reporting reviewed for this corrected card documents who was dismissed, but does not establish that causal allegation or identify impeachment testimony as the reason. The account therefore names only the documented personnel actions and leaves motive unresolved. It does not characterize the changes as retaliation, a purge of witnesses, or proof of political loyalty. No conclusion about legality or resulting readiness effects is drawn. This correction preserves the dated leadership-change event while removing unsupported participants and motive.

terminal_record.description_short: The UAE defense ministry reported cumulative missile and drone totals on March 3; the supplied Trump connection remains unverified.
terminal_record.description_medium: In a March 3, 2026 briefing, the UAE Ministry of Defence said its air defenses had dealt with 186 ballistic missiles since Iranian attacks began: 172 were destroyed, 13 fell into the sea, and one landed in UAE territory. terminal_record.description_long: On March 3, 2026, the UAE Ministry of Defence reported cumulative air-defense figures for attacks since Iranian attacks began. It said the country had dealt with 186 ballistic missiles, destroying 172; 13 fell into the sea and one landed in the UAE. Officials also reported 812 Iranian drones detected, 755 intercepted and 57 landing within the country, along with eight cruise missiles detected and destroyed. The statement said the attacks caused three fatalities, 68 minor injuries and limited damage to certain civilian facilities. These are figures attributed to UAE officials; they are not a count of attacks occurring on March 3 and were not independently audited in the supplied excerpt. Reuters's later March 9 cutoff cannot be used as a March 3 snapshot. The record's earlier Trump escalation framing is not established by the material: it does not show Trump directed the attacks or the UAE briefing. No target location is identified for each projectile, and any causal link to a Trump decision remains unverified. This is an internal account of the briefing, not a finding about Trump's role.

terminal_record.title: Trump Acknowledged Istanbul Business Conflict in 2015 Interview
terminal_record.description_short: Trump said a major Istanbul building gave him “a little conflict of interest” when discussing Turkey in a 2015 interview.
terminal_record.description_medium: In a December 1, 2015 interview on Breitbart News Daily, Donald Trump said he had “a little conflict of interest” because of a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. This supports a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not establish repeated Turkish-government bookings at the Istanbul property or that the business interest shaped U.S. policy toward Turkey.
terminal_record.description_long: On December 1, 2015, Donald Trump spoke on Breitbart News Daily about Turkey and said he had “a little conflict of interest” because he had a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. TIME later quoted the remark and identified it as a 2015 interview; Politico reported on a Tuesday-morning Breitbart interview on December 1, 2015. The statement documents a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not show that Turkish government agencies or affiliated groups booked Trump Towers Istanbul during his presidency, that those bookings generated payments to Trump, or that U.S. decisions toward Turkey were made to benefit the property. The held record further alleges that Trump repeatedly favored President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan because of this business interest. The sources accessed for this repair do not establish that causal link. This account therefore records the 2015 statement and leaves the broader booking and policy-influence allegations unresolved; it does not present them as findings of corruption or proof that the property changed government policy.
terminal_record.date_precision: Politico reports the Breitbart interview on December 1, 2015; TIME independently dates the quoted interview to 2015.

terminal_record.title: Bondi Calls for DOJ Working Group to Review Trump and Jan. 6 Cases
terminal_record.description_short: AP reported that after her February 5 swearing-in, Bondi called for a DOJ group to review Trump and Jan. 6 prosecutions.
terminal_record.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general on February 5, 2025, and hours later called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize Jack Smith’s work and review prosecutions stemming from January 6. The report documents a review directive, not a January 20 order to dismiss cases against Trump allies.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 5, 2025, the Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general and, hours later, called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize the work of special counsel Jack Smith, who had charged Donald Trump in two criminal cases, and review what Bondi described as “unethical prosecutions” stemming from the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. The supplied original entry instead claimed that Bondi ordered DOJ to drop or suspend a broad set of cases against Trump allies on January 20, including fraud and campaign-finance matters. The date is incompatible with AP’s account of Bondi taking office on February 5, and the AP article describes reviews rather than case dismissals. This correction records the same-day directive AP documents and does not claim that cases were dismissed. It also does not treat the act of reviewing cases as proof of misconduct. The record does not establish which cases, if any, the working group later recommended for action or what outcomes followed.

proposed_survivor_patch.description_long: During the January 2017 inauguration, the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee booked rooms, meals and event space at Trump International Hotel in Washington. In December 2018, WNYC and ProPublica reported on interviews, internal emails and receipts documenting the committee’s payments to the Trump Organization and a dispute over event-space pricing. The hotel’s managing director offered $175,000 per day for ballroom and meeting-room use, or $700,000 for four days. An inaugural planner questioned the proposed rates, and the article said it was unclear what amount the committee ultimately paid for the rental. This evidence documents a commercial relationship and a pricing concern; it does not establish the Trump Organization’s net profit, a hundreds-of-thousands amount earned during inauguration weekend, or a final determination that the prices violated law. A separate D.C. attorney general complaint filed in 2020 alleged overpayment for event space, but its allegations belong to a later lawsuit record and are not proof of the frozen row’s weekend-profit claim. The event description should remain limited to payments and price negotiations documented in the reporting.

terminal_record.title: The Atlantic’s “Unthinkable” Project Ranked 50 Trump-Era Incidents
terminal_record.description_short: The Atlantic catalogued 50 incidents from Trump’s first term, ranking them subjectively by outlandishness and importance.
terminal_record.description_medium: The Atlantic described its “Unthinkable” project as a catalog of 50 incidents from the midpoint of Trump’s first term, ranked subjectively for outlandishness and importance. A linked explainer was published January 14, 2019. The available material supports the magazine’s editorial project and framing, not a measured democratic-stability effect or a continuing risk signal in March 2026.
terminal_record.description_long: The Atlantic’s landing page introduces “Donald Trump’s 50 Most Unthinkable Moments” as a review of 50 incidents from the first Trump presidency. The magazine says it chose incidents it considered improbable, norm-bending, and destructive, and explicitly describes its ranking as highly subjective, based on outlandishness and importance. A linked video explainer featuring editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg was published January 14, 2019, and explains the project as an attempt to chronicle bizarre and dangerous moments of the presidency. These sources document an editorial catalog and the publication’s own description of its selection. They do not show that the magazine measured democratic stability, identified a mitigation plan, or continued to issue a specific risk signal in March 2026. The frozen record’s March 4, 2026 date and continuing-risk wording are not retained because the accessible evidence connects the project to the 2019 midterm of Trump’s first term. January 14 is the linked explainer’s publication date and earliest archive capture date for the landing page; the landing page’s original release timestamp remains uncertain. This entry describes editorial coverage, not an independent finding of harm.

terminal_record.title: Trump's February 25 Memorandum Targets Covington & Burling
terminal_record.description_short: Trump's February 25, 2025 memorandum directed clearance suspensions for specified Covington lawyers and federal reviews of the firm's engagements and contracts.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 25, 2025, Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum directing agencies to suspend specified Covington & Burling security clearances pending review, terminate federal engagements where permitted by law, and have OMB review the firm's contracts. The source identifies a memorandum, not a March 14 executive order. The documents establish directives, not their eventual implementation or outcome.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 25, 2025, Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum titled “Suspension of Security Clearances and Evaluation of Government Contracts.” It directed executive departments and agencies to take lawful steps to suspend active clearances held by Peter Koski and Covington & Burling members, partners, and employees who assisted former Special Counsel Jack Smith, pending a review of their roles and responsibilities. The memo also directed agencies to take steps to terminate Covington engagements to the maximum extent permitted by law and consistent with a separate Office of Management and Budget memorandum. It instructed OMB to issue a memorandum directing all agencies to review government contracts with the firm. The White House described the action as a memorandum and stated its rationale in terms of “weaponization of the judicial process”; that is the administration’s stated justification, not an independently established finding about the lawyers. The official documents verify issuance and the directions. They do not show whether clearances were ultimately suspended, contracts ended, or engagements terminated. The stored March 14, 2025 date and “executive order” label are incorrect for this action. This record covers the February 25 memorandum and its stated directives only.

February 25, 2025

MEMORANDUM FOR THE SECRETARY OF STATE THE SECRETARY OF DEFENSE THE ATTORNEY GENERAL THE SECRETARY OF ENERGY THE DIRECTOR OF THE OFFICE OF MANAGEMENT AND BUDGET THE DIRECTOR OF NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE THE DIRECTOR OF THE CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY THE DIRECTOR OF THE OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT

SUBJECT: Suspension of Security Clearances and Evaluation of Government Contracts I hereby direct the Attorney General and all other relevant heads of executive departments and agencies (agencies) to immediately take steps consistent with applicable law to suspend any active security clearances held by Peter Koski and all members, partners, and employees of Covington & Burling LLP who assisted former Special Counsel Jack Smith during his time as Special Counsel, pending a review and determination of their roles and responsibilities, if any, in the weaponization of the judicial process. I also direct the Attorney General and heads of agencies to take such actions as are necessary to terminate any engagement of Covington & Burling LLP by any agency to the maximum extent permitted by law and consistent with the memorandum that shall be issued by the Director of the Office of Management and Budget. Additionally, if any of the covered Covington & Burling LLP members, partners, and employees referenced in this memorandum obtained a security clearance from an agency not included as an addressee of this memorandum, the Director of the Office of Personnel Management shall provide this memorandum to the appropriate clearance-granting agency to ensure compliance. I further direct the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to issue a memorandum to all agencies to review all Government contracts with Covington & Burling LLP.

terminal_record.title: ProPublica Reported GOP Committees Spent at Trump Properties; RNC Said Rates Were Market
terminal_record.description_short: ProPublica documented political committee spending at Trump properties; an RNC official said the properties charged market rates.
terminal_record.description_medium: ProPublica’s May 2018 analysis of Federal Election Commission filings reported at least $3.1 million in political committee spending at Trump Organization properties since the 2016 election. It listed at least $945,027 in Republican National Committee spending, mostly for fundraising and political-event venues. An anonymous RNC official said the properties charged market rates. The reporting supports the spending and conflict context, not the frozen claim that committees generally paid above-market rates.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 4, 2018, ProPublica reported that political committees had spent at least $3.1 million at Trump Organization properties since the 2016 presidential election, based on expenditure reports submitted to the Federal Election Commission. It said the vast majority of that spending came from Republican-connected committees. ProPublica listed at least $1,684,700 in post-election spending by Donald J. Trump for President and at least $945,027 by the Republican National Committee, mostly for fundraising and political-event venues. An anonymous RNC official told ProPublica that the properties charged the committee market rates. These records support a narrower account of political committees directing reported spending to properties owned by the president’s company while he held office. They do not support the frozen entry’s allegation that committees generally paid above-market prices or its claim of tens of millions in such payments. The market-rate statement is an attributed defense, not an independent price comparison. ProPublica also notes that its dataset covered electronic FEC filings and excluded some committees that filed on paper, so the figures are not a complete count of all political spending.
terminal_record.date_basis: The source reports spending since the 2016 election and was published May 4, 2018; this is the reported period, not a verified first transaction date.

terminal_record.title: WBUR Interviewed Atlantic Editors About Their 50-Moment Trump Project
terminal_record.description_short: A January 2019 WBUR interview described The Atlantic’s 50-moment project and its focus on presidential norm-breaking.
terminal_record.description_medium: On January 14, 2019, WBUR interviewed Atlantic editors about “Unthinkable,” a special report surveying 50 moments from Donald Trump’s first two years. Editor Adrienne LaFrance described its frame as the “shattering of norms” in presidential communication and treatment of institutions. The interview supports that editorial framing, not a proposal for institutional redesign.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 14, 2019, WBUR published an interview with editors from The Atlantic about the magazine’s “Unthinkable” package on Donald Trump’s first two years in office. WBUR described a special report of 50 moments, and Atlantic editor Adrienne LaFrance said the project’s framing was a “shattering of norms” across Trump’s communication and approach to institutions. She said the team reviewed the first two years and narrowed hundreds of candidate moments to 50. The revised description identifies the project and attributes its interpretation to the editors. The supplied record’s claim that this was a continuing structural diagnosis leading readers from rebuttal toward institutional redesign is not supported by this interview. The source documents editorial framing and a curated list; it does not identify a specific constitutional reform, establish that Atlantic described a single ongoing pattern as structural, or measure institutional effects. The frozen date of March 4, 2026 does not match the cited 2019 material. This card dates the documented interview to January 14, 2019 and leaves the package’s exact initial publication date unspecified.

And so the reporters and editors at The Atlantic have put together a special report that tries to take stock of this presidency with a cool head and clear eyes. Thanks to them, we have a look at what they describe as 50 extraordinary moments in an extraordinary presidency.

It happens in sort of small ways and then very big ways, and so I think, day-to-day, it can be hard to attach a weight to whatever it is that has happened, but looking back over two years — I mean, we had a research team comb through every single day of the first two years of the presidency and we had, at first, hundreds of moments that we wanted to parse down from. We wound up with 50.”

children.description_short: SSA said it revoked DOGE Team 1 access to PII systems under a March 20 court order; its declaration says DOGE defendants never accessed SSA systems of record.
children.description_medium: On March 24, Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek told a court that SSA had revoked SSA DOGE Team 1 members’ access to systems containing personally identifiable information under the court’s March 20 temporary restraining order. The declaration names Enterprise Data Warehouse, Numident, Master Beneficiary Record and Supplemental Security Record, while stating that DOGE defendants had never accessed SSA systems of record.
children.description_long: On March 24, 2025, Acting Social Security Administration Commissioner Leland Dudek filed a declaration supporting the status report required by the court’s March 20 temporary restraining order. He wrote that SSA had revoked all SSA DOGE Team 1 members’ access to systems containing personally identifiable information or systems of record. The declaration names the Enterprise Data Warehouse, Numident, Master Beneficiary Record, and Supplemental Security Record. It separately states that DOGE defendants had never had access to SSA systems of record. This evidence supports a narrow account of SSA’s access restrictions and reported compliance; it does not establish which individual previously viewed which information, whether data was copied or misused, or that the court made a final finding of unlawful access. The event is distinct from the February Treasury letter: Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service described read-only access to its payment-system data, whereas this declaration concerns SSA systems and a separate court order. The supplied February 18 date therefore does not describe either child accurately. Use March 24 for this declaration-based event and preserve the distinction between SSA DOGE Team 1 members and DOGE defendants, whom the declaration says had never accessed SSA systems of record.

terminal_record.title: DOGE Access Concerns at the Energy Department Raise NNSA Questions
terminal_record.description_short: Reuters reported DOE access concerns about DOGE staff; DOE said they had not accessed classified information, including NNSA material.
terminal_record.description_medium: Reuters reported on February 7, 2025, that three DOGE members had begun working at the Department of Energy while officials worried they could access personnel files and other systems. On February 12, DOE told Reuters no DOGE employee had accessed or been granted access to classified information or facilities, including NNSA classified information. The reporting does not establish access to NNSA personnel files.
terminal_record.description_long:
Reuters reported on February 7, 2025, that three members of the Department of Government Efficiency had started working at the U.S. Department of Energy. Two sources told Reuters that DOE officials were concerned the staffers could gain access to personnel files, federal-grant information, and financial-management systems. Reuters also reported that one DOGE member worked in the chief information officer’s office and that all three appeared in DOE email and messaging systems. This supports a reported access concern at DOE, not a finding that DOGE had opened NNSA personnel files.

On February 12, Reuters reported that two lawmakers asked DOE whether DOGE had access to nuclear information. A department spokesperson said no DOGE employees had accessed or been granted access to classified information or facilities, including classified NNSA information. That statement addresses classified data and facilities; it does not resolve every question about possible access to unclassified DOE human-resources systems. The available reporting does not show that NNSA personnel records were accessed, that files were misused, or that any foreign-intelligence targeting occurred. The corrected entry records the access concern and the department’s denial without presenting the alleged NNSA-file access as established.

children.title: Kennedy Removes All 17 Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Panel
children.description_short: Kennedy removed all 17 members of CDC's vaccine advisory panel on June 9, 2025.
children.description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and said they would be replaced. Reuters reported that vaccine scientists protested the move and that experts warned it could undermine public confidence in health agencies. This child records the panel action only; it does not describe the committee as dissolved or characterize all replacement members.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). Reuters reported that Kennedy was in the process of replacing them and that many vaccine scientists protested the decision. The committee advises the CDC on how vaccines are used and by whom. Reuters also reported that the members had been appointed during the Biden administration, including 13 in 2024, and that without their removal the Trump administration would not have been able to choose a majority of the committee until 2028. Kennedy described the change as part of restoring public trust; experts quoted by Reuters said the dismissal could undermine confidence in health agencies. That is an attributed warning, not evidence that public confidence or vaccine access measurably changed. The CDC said the panel’s next meeting would take place June 25–27 in Atlanta. This record covers the June committee-removal action only. The source describes members being replaced, not ACIP being dissolved, and the supplied broad label for replacement members is not repeated. HHS’s release also describes ACIP as making recommendations on vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need to CDC.

WASHINGTON, June 9 (Reuters) - Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has fired all 17 members of a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention panel of vaccine experts and is in the process of replacing them, his department said on Monday, drawing protest from many vaccine scientists.

All 17 ACIP members were appointed under former President Joe Biden's administration, including 13 in 2024, HHS said. Without their removal, Trump's administration would not have been able to choose a majority of the committee until 2028.

The CDC panel will convene its next meeting June 25-27 at CDC headquarters in Atlanta, the department said.

children.title: HHS Layoffs Begin at NIH During a Planned 1,200-Position Reduction
children.description_short: HHS layoffs began at NIH on April 1, 2025; the department's plan targeted about 1,200 NIH positions.
children.description_medium: HHS began broad health-agency layoffs on April 1, 2025, and Reuters reported that the National Institutes of Health was among the affected agencies, with NIH employees notified of layoffs that morning. HHS’s restructuring fact sheet separately said the plan would reduce NIH’s workforce by approximately 1,200 through centralized support functions. The plan figure is a target, not proof that exactly 1,200 people were dismissed.
children.description_long: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs across federal health agencies. Reuters reported that the cuts affected the National Institutes of Health and that NIH employees had been notified early that morning that they were laid off. HHS’s restructuring fact sheet described a planned NIH workforce reduction of approximately 1,200 employees through the centralization of procurement, human resources, and communications across its 27 institutes and centers. The figure is the department’s plan, not a verified count of completed dismissals. Reuters described a broader 10,000-person reduction across health agencies, not 10,000 NIH layoffs. The supplied February 20 entry merged this workforce action with the separate June removal of ACIP members; this child isolates the NIH-related layoffs and uses the April 1 date. The source material does not establish that hundreds of the affected NIH workers were scientists, identify the number of researchers who lost jobs, or measure any resulting research interruption. It also does not show that all planned NIH reductions occurred. The record therefore describes the confirmed start of layoffs and the department’s stated target separately, without converting the target into an outcome.

terminal_record.description_long:
On June 9, 2025, HHS announced that Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the CDC advisory committee that makes recommendations about vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need. HHS said new members were under consideration and framed the decision as an effort to restore public trust in vaccines.

Reuters reported that the entire 17-member panel was being replaced and that many vaccine scientists protested the move. HHS said the members had been appointed during the Biden administration, including 13 in 2024, and argued that without their removal the Trump administration would not have been able to choose a committee majority until 2028. These are the agency’s stated rationale and reported reaction. The sources establish the committee’s removal, but they do not show what recommendations followed or measure any resulting change in vaccine uptake, safety, or health outcomes. This entry records the personnel and advisory-structure change without treating the agency’s rationale or critics’ concerns as a proven public-health consequence.

terminal_record.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization and directing prospective funding and personnel changes. The supplied materials describe a separate UNESCO withdrawal announcement on July 22, with withdrawal expected at the end of December 2026, while a February 4 order called for a review. The UNESCO statement could not be read, so those details remain unverified. The frozen record combines different dates and actions.
terminal_record.description_long:
On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. The order directed officials to pause future U.S. funding and support, recall or reassign personnel and contractors working with WHO, identify partners for necessary activities, and stop negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not say that U.S. membership ended that day, and this draft makes no claim about resulting health effects.

The frozen record also says the United States withdrew from UNESCO on January 20. The supplied research materials instead place a separate UNESCO withdrawal announcement on July 22, 2025, with an effective date at the end of December 2026, and describe the February 4, 2025 executive order as directing a review of U.S. support to international organizations. Those UNESCO details remain unverified here: the cited page returned a human-verification screen, and the supplied account does not independently prove the announcement or effective date. This internal draft separates the events and marks the UNESCO claim as unverified. The parent remains ineligible for publication.

candidate_children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed the Secretary of State and Office of Management and Budget to pause future U.S. funds, support and resources to WHO; recall and reassign government personnel or contractors working with the organization; and identify U.S. and international partners to assume necessary WHO activities. The order also directed the Secretary of State to cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. This is an order to pursue withdrawal, not proof that the United States left WHO on January 20. The frozen entry incorrectly said the country withdrew from both WHO and UNESCO that day; the UNESCO action is a separate later claim and is kept in a second internal draft. The order's text does not establish the broader outcome claims in the frozen synopsis, so this card does not state that U.S. departure had already removed the country from disease-surveillance networks or produced quantified public-health harms.

terminal_record.title: DHS Rescinds Protected-Areas Guidance for Immigration Enforcement
terminal_record.description_short: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded 2021 guidance limiting immigration enforcement in or near protected areas.
terminal_record.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued a memorandum rescinding the 2021 guidance for immigration enforcement in or near protected areas. DHS said the change applied to ICE and CBP and directed officers to use enforcement discretion without the prior bright-line rules. This supports a policy change, not claims that Tom Homan personally ordered raids or that specific collateral harms occurred.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine C. Huffman issued an immediate memorandum titled “Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.” The memo superseded and rescinded the October 27, 2021 DHS guidance for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection actions in or near areas previously designated for special protection. The memo says officers should continue using enforcement discretion and states that agency heads need not create “bright line rules” about where immigration laws may be enforced. DHS described the change as rescinding the Biden administration’s guidelines for enforcement in or near “sensitive” areas, including schools and churches. These records establish a change to department policy and expanded discretion at those locations. They do not establish that Border Czar Tom Homan personally ordered raids at churches or schools, how many such operations occurred, that families were separated as a result, or that advocates documented hundreds of collateral-harm cases. This entry is limited to the documented rescission and avoids turning a change in enforcement guidance into an unsupported account of specific raids or outcomes.

January 20,2025

MEMORANDUM FOR: Caleb Vitello

Acting Director U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement

Pete R.Flores

Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Commissioner U.S. Customs and Border Protection

FROM: Benjamine C. Huffman Acting Secretary

SUBJECT: Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas

This memorandum addresses Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions in or near areas that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) previously determined require special protection. It is effective immediately. This memorandum supersedes and rescinds Alejandro Mayorkas's October 27, 2021 memorandum entitled, Guidelines for Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.

source_fact_map.fact: The memo no longer required agency heads to create bright-line rules governing where immigration enforcement may occur.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Going forward, law enforcement officers should continue to use that discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense. It is not necessary, however, for the head of the agency to create bright line rules regarding where our immigration laws are permitted to be enforced. The Director of ICE and the Commissioner of CBP may wish to issue further guidance to assist officers in exercising appropriate enforcement discretion.

Release Date: January 21, 2025

WASHINGTON – Yesterday, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued two directives. terminal_record.title: Vought Ordered CFPB Staff to Stop Work; Court Blocked Further Layoffs
terminal_record.description_short: Vought ordered CFPB staff to stop work on Feb. 10, 2025; a judge blocked more layoffs after over 100 workers had been fired.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 10, 2025, Acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work. A federal judge later blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had been fired that week. The sources support a work stoppage and workforce reduction effort, but do not substantiate the frozen entry’s claim that all roughly 1,700 employees were fired on February 7.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 10, 2025, CFPB Acting Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work, according to the District Court’s later account in NTEU v. Vought. The court said the administration was pursuing measures to dismantle the agency, including firings, funding cuts, contract terminations, office closures and a reduction in force. On February 14, NPR reported that a federal judge blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had already been fired that week. The record therefore describes a serious work stoppage and attempted workforce reduction, not a completed firing of the bureau’s full roughly 1,700-person staff. The original February 7 date is not the date of the stop-work order identified in the opinion, and the sources reviewed do not establish that all pending CFPB cases were halted. The injunction was preliminary while litigation continued; it does not by itself decide every underlying legal question. This correction preserves the CFPB action and its immediate legal response while separating completed events from planned reductions. The supplied claim that the bureau’s closure benefited Trump campaign donors is not supported by the sources cited here and is omitted.

terminal_record.title: ICE solicitation sought online monitoring and facial-recognition capability
terminal_record.description_short: A February 2025 report described an ICE contractor solicitation for social-media monitoring and facial-recognition capability.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 11, 2025, The Intercept reported that ICE was soliciting contractor proposals to monitor online discussion of the agency and its leaders. The contract documents also requested facial-recognition capability to search for information about a photographed subject. The source describes a proposed procurement, not a deployed mass-identification system, and does not establish targeting of undocumented immigrants or political dissenters.
terminal_record.description_long: This repair narrows the frozen entry to a contractor solicitation reported by The Intercept on February 11, 2025. The article, citing contract documents, says ICE planned to monitor and locate negative social-media discussion about the agency and senior officials. It also quotes a request for facial-recognition capability that could use a subject’s photograph to search the internet for associated information. Those details support a proposal for online monitoring and identity research. They do not establish that a system was awarded, deployed, or used to identify undocumented immigrants across multiple platforms. The source also does not establish that ICE selected political dissenters as targets; it describes monitoring discussion of ICE and its leadership and frames the procurement around threats to personnel and facilities. The original card’s claims of a live mass-identification program, database matching, and disproportionate targeting are therefore removed. This is a serious privacy and speech concern at the proposal stage, with implementation and actual effects unresolved.

proposed_survivor_patch.description_long: On April 6, 2017, Chinese authorities granted preliminary approval to three trademark applications from Ivanka Trump’s company, according to CNN and Associated Press excerpts supplied in the source-worker packet. AP reported that the approvals coincided with Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner dining with Xi Jinping and his wife at Mar-a-Lago. CNN identified the marks as covering jewelry, spa services and bags, based on Chinese trademark documents it reviewed. The 16 mentioned in the earlier account referred to marks the company already held as fully registered; it was not the number newly approved that day. CNN’s report was published April 18, while AP’s follow-up appeared April 19, so those dates describe reporting rather than the approval event. The timing raised an ethics question because Ivanka Trump held a White House advisory role while her company received foreign trademark approvals. The supplied excerpts do not show that Donald or Ivanka Trump intervened in the process, that the dinner caused the approvals, that officials treated the applications improperly, or that the approvals produced a particular commercial return. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said trademark applications were handled according to law and equal-protection principles. This account records the approvals and their timing while leaving any allegation of favoritism unproven.

terminal_record.description_long: On March 27, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the State Department may have revoked more than 300 visas. The Associated Press reported that Ozturk's lawyer said no charges had been filed. AP also reported that she was one of four students who wrote a Tufts Daily opinion piece criticizing the university's response to demands for divestment from companies tied to Israel. Reuters reported Rubio did not explain what specific conduct by Ozturk justified revoking her visa. He listed vandalism, harassment, building takeovers and other disruptive conduct as grounds for taking away student visas, but did not say Ozturk had done those things. He said the standard in her case involved support for movements contrary to U.S. foreign policy. The reporting does not show that every visa in the reported total was revoked for criticism of Israel, for a social media post, or for one common reason; it leaves individual grounds unresolved.

corrected_proposal_for_survivor.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order immediately reinstating the 2020 Schedule F order and renaming the category “Schedule Policy/Career.” The order directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations and issue guidance on additional positions for agencies to consider. corrected_proposal_for_survivor.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed “Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce.” Section 2 immediately reinstated Executive Order 13957, the 2020 order creating Schedule F, subject to amendments in the new order. Those amendments replaced the excepted-service schedule label “F” with “Policy/Career” and directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations that could impede implementation. The order also directed OPM to issue, within 30 days, guidance about additional position categories agencies should consider recommending for inclusion. It says employees in or applicants for these positions need not personally or politically support the President, but are required to faithfully implement administration policies; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal. These are the signed order’s rules and directions. The accessed document does not establish how many positions were later reclassified, how many employees lost protections, or whether any specific person was dismissed under it. This record describes the enacted policy mechanism, not a completed workforce purge or an asserted list of political enemies.

terminal_record.title: Kushner's Initial SF-86 Omitted Foreign-Government Contacts
terminal_record.description_short: Kushner's initial SF-86 omitted foreign-government contacts; the 100+ figure was reported later.
terminal_record.description_medium: Jared Kushner’s initial SF-86 was submitted on January 18, 2017, and omitted foreign-government contacts, according to his later statement and his lawyer’s comments to Politico. He said supplemental information followed the next day. The figure of more than 100 contacts was reported in July 2017, so it does not belong to the record’s May 25 date.
terminal_record.description_long: Jared Kushner submitted his initial SF-86 security questionnaire on January 18, 2017. In a July statement to the Senate Judiciary Committee, he said the filing was a rough draft submitted prematurely after his assistant misunderstood a message; the form did not list any foreign-government contacts. He said supplemental information was sent the next day. His explanation is attributed to him and does not independently establish why the form was incomplete. On July 16, Politico quoted Kushner’s attorney Jamie Gorelick saying the original submission omitted all contacts with foreign-government officials and that later materials included more than 100 calls or meetings with representatives of more than 20 countries. That later figure should not be assigned to the May 25 date in the source record: it was reported in July, months after the initial form. This repair dates the event to the January 18 filing and places the 100+ figure in the later supplementation context. The available material establishes the omission and reported correction, but not deliberate concealment, any particular clearance outcome, or the original synopsis’s suggestion that the contacts materially affected the FBI counterintelligence inquiry.

terminal_record.title: P.L. 119-21 Retains Lawful Permanent Residents on SNAP Eligibility List
terminal_record.description_short: The 2025 law’s SNAP eligibility list expressly includes lawful permanent residents.
terminal_record.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025, rewrote SNAP’s noncitizen eligibility subsection. Its list expressly includes lawful permanent residents, so the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The accessed statutory text does not establish the number affected or verify the supplied note about the existing five-year bar.
terminal_record.description_long: On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 amended section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, SNAP’s eligibility provision. The amendment lists who may qualify: U.S. citizens or nationals; lawful permanent residents; people granted Cuban and Haitian entrant status; and people lawfully residing under a Compact of Free Association. It also says an individual must be a U.S. resident and a household must otherwise qualify under section 6. Because lawful permanent residents appear expressly in the enacted list, the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The text does not establish how many people lost eligibility or the effects on food access, and this card makes no numerical impact claim. The supplied research note says a prior five-year bar continues to apply to some lawful permanent residents, but I did not verify that detail in the text accessed here, so it is excluded from the asserted description. The source resolves the title’s blanket statement; it does not by itself establish every category that lost eligibility compared with prior law.

source_fact_map.fact: Section 10108 addresses alien SNAP eligibility and amends Food and Nutrition Act section 6(f).
source_fact_map.quote: SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.

    Section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (7 U.S.C. 
2015(f)) is amended to read as follows:
    ``(f) No individual who is a member of a household otherwise 
eligible to participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
under this section shall be eligible to participate in the supplemental 
nutrition assistance program as a member of that or any other household 
unless he or she is--
            ``(1) a resident of the United States; and
            ``(2) either--
                    ``(A) a citizen or national of the United States;
                    ``(B) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent 
                residence as an immigrant as defined by sections 
                101(a)(15) and 101(a)(20) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act, excluding, among others, alien 
                visitors, tourists, diplomats, and students who enter 
                the United States temporarily with no intention of 
                abandoning their residence in a foreign country;
                    ``(C) an alien who has been granted the status of 
                Cuban and Haitian entrant, as defined in section 501(e) 
                of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Public 
                Law 96-422); or
                    ``(D) an individual who lawfully resides in the 
                United States in accordance with a Compact of Free 
                Association referred to in section 402(b)(2)(G) of the 
                Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
                Reconciliation Act of 1996.
        The income (less, at State option, a pro rata share) and 
        financial resources of the individual rendered ineligible to 
        participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
        under this subsection shall be considered in determining the 
        eligibility and the value of the allotment of the household of 
        which such individual is a member.''.

retained_unadopted_draft.title: News Ltd. Planned a 40% Stake in the News of the World After a Pergamon Bid
retained_unadopted_draft.description_short: A 1968 Guardian report described a planned News Ltd. stake in the News of the World after a Pergamon Press takeover bid.
retained_unadopted_draft.description_medium: The Guardian reported on October 25, 1968 that News Ltd. planned to take a 40 per cent stake in the News of the World after Pergamon Press, led by Robert Maxwell, made a takeover bid. The report said Rupert Murdoch was to become joint managing director with Sir William Carr. It does not mention Donald Trump or establish a connection to him.
retained_unadopted_draft.description_long: The Guardian's archive report, published Friday, October 25, 1968, described an arrangement under which News Ltd. was to take a 40 per cent stake in the News of the World after a takeover bid by Pergamon Press, the publishing group headed by Robert Maxwell, was defeated. The report said Rupert Murdoch, then chairman of News Ltd., was to become joint managing director with the newspaper's existing chairman, Sir William Carr. Its wording that the deal was unfolded the previous day places the report of the arrangement on October 24, although the archive item itself is dated October 25. The article describes a British newspaper ownership and management transaction; it does not report a Trump action or relationship. The frozen record's title and synopsis misidentify the newspaper titles and claim a bidding contest involving The Sun, while the accessible Guardian report concerns the News of the World. The linked TrumpFile page was reported in prior research as returning HTTP 202 without readable text. The supplied evidence therefore supports a narrow account of the 1968 transaction but gives no documented reason for placing it in a Trump-focused collection. Keep this copy as an exclusion review draft, not as a Trump-linked entry. The source says the stake and management changes were planned; it does not establish that they were completed.
retained_unadopted_draft.date_basis: The Guardian report is dated 1968-10-25 and says the deal was unfolded 'yesterday'; event date is inferred as 1968-10-24.

In a deal unfolded yesterday to defeat the takeover bid by Pergamon Press, the publishing group headed by Robert Maxwell, MP, the Australian newspaper chain, News Ltd., is to take a 40 per cent stake in the "News of the World." This will be the largest single holding. The chairman of News Ltd., Mr Rupert Murdoch, is to become joint managing director of NoW, with the present chairman, Sir William Carr.

Congressional Research Service and Holland & Knight explain that the cap rose from 30% to 50%; tax advisers said this could help leveraged businesses and private-equity funds. The sources do not substantiate the packet’s $1.5 billion figure or its claim that lobbyists inserted the provision without scrutiny.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 27, 2020, the CARES Act became Public Law 116-136. Section 2306 temporarily raised the cap on deductible business interest from 30 percent to 50 percent for tax years 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service explained that the amendment also let firms use 2019 income when calculating the 2020 cap. Holland & Knight’s April 2020 tax analysis said additional deductions could reduce cash taxes or create or increase net operating losses for highly leveraged businesses, including private-equity funds and their portfolio companies. This supports a narrow description of the law’s tax treatment of borrowing costs and its potential benefit to leveraged firms. The sources do not establish the frozen entry’s $1.5 billion estimate, lobbyist authorship, or claim that the provision was inserted without committee scrutiny. Those allegations are omitted rather than treated as facts. The card describes an enacted, broadly applicable tax rule and does not infer that private equity alone received it or that the change produced a particular realized benefit.

terminal_record.title: VA Says DOGE Has Not Accessed Veterans' Personal Records Amid Privacy Concerns
terminal_record.description_short: NPR reported uncertainty about a DOGE staffer's VA data access and the department's denial; the supplied claim of a completed breach is unsupported.
terminal_record.description_medium: An NPR report published March 11, 2025, said a DOGE staffer had been present at VA while a current employee could not confirm what data the staffer could access. VA's spokesperson said DOGE had not accessed veterans' or beneficiaries' data, and the department's written reply to a Senate inquiry said DOGE had no access to veterans' personal records. The evidence documents concern and denial, not a confirmed breach.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 11, 2025, NPR reported questions about DOGE's access to sensitive information held by federal agencies. For VA, NPR quoted a current agency employee saying a DOGE staffer had been present and that the scope of data access was unclear. The employee requested anonymity because of possible retaliation. A VA spokesperson told NPR that DOGE did not have and had not had access to veterans' or beneficiaries' data. In a written response to the Senate Committee on Veterans' Affairs about DOGE access to VA systems and sensitive information, VA likewise stated that DOGE did not have access to veterans' personal records. These sources support an access concern, the presence of a DOGE staffer, and an official denial. They do not establish that medical files were viewed, PTSD or combat-injury diagnoses were exposed, millions of records were accessed, or veterans' organizations filed lawsuits over a confirmed breach. The frozen card's breach language should be removed; its specific allegations remain unverified and contradicted by VA's statements.

terminal_record.description_medium: This internal draft concerns Mordechai Vanunu’s 1986 disclosure about Israel’s nuclear program and a disputed allegation that publisher Robert Maxwell alerted Israeli officials. BBC and Independent reporting support the disclosure’s historical context. The allegation about Maxwell is attributed to Ari Ben-Menashe and was denied by Maxwell. The supplied record gives no documented connection to Donald Trump, and its September 20 date is not established by the sources accessed.
terminal_record.description_long: This is an internal historical draft about Mordechai Vanunu’s 1986 disclosure of information and photographs concerning Israel’s Dimona nuclear program, plus a separate, disputed allegation about publisher Robert Maxwell. BBC and Independent reporting describe Vanunu’s disclosure and subsequent events. A later Independent report attributes the Maxwell tip claim to Ari Ben-Menashe and reports Maxwell rejecting it; that account does not establish Maxwell’s role as fact. The frozen record begins with “Trump:” but the supplied packet provides no source tying Donald Trump to Vanunu, Maxwell, the Sunday Times disclosure, or the alleged alert. The frozen date, September 20, 1986, is not corroborated by the accessed chronology: BBC dates the Sunday Times story to October 5, while the Independent describes the disclosure as occurring in 1986. The TrumpFile URL previously returned HTTP 202 with an empty body and the New York Times URL returned HTTP 403, according to the supplied notes. Keep this internal draft unpublished until its Trump relevance, intended event, and date are resolved.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Ben-Menashe also claimed that, in 1986, Maxwell tipped off the Israeli embassy in London that Mordechai Vanunu, the nuclear scientist later jailed for 18 years in Israel, had given information about Israel's nuclear capability to The Sunday Times, then to the Daily Mirror. No news organisation would publish Ben-Menashe's story at first, because of Maxwell's famed litigiousness. But later an MP asked a question about the claims in the House of Commons, which meant that newspapers were able to report what had been said without fear of being sued for libel. Just days before he died Maxwell called the claims "ludicrous, a total invention".

terminal_record.title: Trump promoted a $59.99 branded Bible; $300 million in revenue is unsupported
terminal_record.description_short: Trump promoted the $59.99 God Bless the USA Bible; AP reporting does not substantiate the $300 million revenue claim.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 26, 2024, Trump promoted the God Bless the USA Bible and urged supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. AP later reported close to 120,000 copies shipped to the United States from China by late March and estimated about $7 million in potential retail sales at the minimum price. AP also cited a disclosure showing $300,000 in CIC Ventures Bible royalties, while noting the period and any additional payments were unclear. The $300 million revenue claim is unsupported by these reports.
terminal_record.description_long:
On March 26, 2024, Donald Trump promoted the “God Bless the USA Bible,” urging supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. The website said Trump’s name and image were used under a paid license from CIC Ventures, a company he reported owning. The book combined a King James Version Bible with U.S. founding documents and the Pledge of Allegiance.

The original title’s $300 million revenue figure is not substantiated by the reporting reviewed here. In October 2024, the Associated Press reported that trade records showed close to 120,000 copies shipped from China to the United States between early February and late March. At the minimum retail price, AP estimated potential sales revenue for those shipments at about $7 million. AP also cited a financial disclosure showing $300,000 in Bible royalties earned by CIC Ventures, while stating that the disclosure period and any additional payments were unclear. Shipment estimates, potential retail sales, company royalties, and Trump’s total receipts are different measures; these reports do not establish total eventual sales or payments. The corrected entry records the promotion and licensing arrangement, removes the unsupported $300 million claim, and leaves final revenue and total royalties unknown.

terminal_record.title: CBP's Electronic-Device Search Policy Predates the 2025 Claim
terminal_record.description_short: DHS announced electronic-media border-search directives in 2009; the record does not establish a February 2025 expansion.
terminal_record.description_medium: DHS announced directives governing searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry in August 2009. The eCFR separately defines “reasonable distance” for immigration officers as within 100 air miles of a U.S. external boundary, and a 2008 ACLU report traces that regulation to 1953. These sources establish a preexisting framework, not a February 2025 Trump action ending Fourth Amendment protections or expanding device searches. The claimed thousands of court challenges remain unsupported.
terminal_record.description_long: On August 27, 2009, the Department of Homeland Security announced directives for searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry. DHS described the policy as consistent with its border authority over non-electronic materials. Separately, the eCFR defines “reasonable distance” under section 287(a)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act as within 100 air miles from an external boundary, while a 2008 ACLU report says the regulation establishing the 100-mile zone was adopted in 1953. These sources show that electronic-media border-search guidance and the 100-mile immigration regulation predate the alleged February 2025 policy. They do not establish that Trump ended Fourth Amendment protections, expanded an electronic-device search zone in February 2025, or caused thousands of court challenges. The frozen entry also combines the statutory operating distance for immigration officers with electronic-device searches; the accessed material does not show that the two authorities are interchangeable. This replacement narrows the card to the documented policy background and leaves the claimed 2025 action unsupported.

terminal_record.title: Unverified Claim That Robert Maxwell Aided Mogilevich's Passport and Banking Network
terminal_record.description_short: Unverified TrumpFile allegation that Robert Maxwell helped Mogilevich obtain passports and banking access.
terminal_record.description_medium: TrumpFile’s timeline alleges that Robert Maxwell arranged Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates in 1988, opened a Bank of New York account used for laundering, and connected Mogilevich with KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov. An FBI report dated August 1996 instead names Shabtai Kalmanovich in connection with passport access. Neither source independently establishes Maxwell’s alleged role or a relationship to Donald Trump.
terminal_record.description_long: TrumpFile labels this account “Robert Maxwell obtains passports for Mogilevich, helps KGB” and dates its timeline item July 1, 1988. The page’s narrative says the alleged passport arrangement happened “sometime in 1988,” and alleges that Maxwell obtained Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates, set up a Bank of New York account for money laundering, and introduced Mogilevich to KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov. These are claims made by TrumpFile, not independently verified findings. A separately accessed text extraction of an FBI report dated August 1996 says Israeli passports had been obtained by Shabtai Kalmanovich for members of organized-crime groups including the Mogilevich organization. That report does not establish Maxwell’s alleged role, the Bank of New York account, or the KGB connection; its reference to Kalmanovich also cautions against treating TrumpFile’s attribution as confirmed. No passport, bank, court, or contemporaneous record confirming Maxwell’s role is supplied. The packet also provides no link between this 1988 allegation and Donald Trump. This internal draft preserves what the supplied timeline alleges while leaving its date at year-level precision and marking the event unverified; the exact day, related outcomes, and asserted Trump relevance remain unresolved.

terminal_record.title: Trump Order Calls for Immigration Detention Pending Proceedings, Subject to Law
terminal_record.description_short: Trump's Jan. 20 order directs detention of removable immigrants pending proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law.
terminal_record.description_medium: Section 10 of the Jan. 20, 2025 order directs DHS to use or establish detention facilities and to detain people apprehended for immigration-law violations pending removal proceedings or removal, to the extent permitted by law. That text supports a detention directive; it does not itself establish indefinite detention without charge, denied bail hearings, or immediate court blocks.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” Section 10 directs the Homeland Security secretary to take appropriate action and use legally available resources or contracts for facilities to detain removable immigrants. It further directs detention of people apprehended for immigration-law violations while removal proceedings are pending or until removal, “to the extent permitted by law.” The order therefore supports describing a federal detention directive tied to removal proceedings and an express legal limitation. The text does not itself say that immigrants may be held indefinitely without charges, instruct immigration judges to deny bail hearings, or report that federal judges immediately blocked the order. The supplied card made those additional claims without providing a court ruling or other supporting source; they are omitted here. The order’s language alone also does not establish how long anyone was detained, how many people were affected, what agencies implemented, or how a court later ruled. This corrected entry records what the signed order says without turning its detention language into unsupported claims about custody duration, court action, or a legal finding.

terminal_record.description_long: On May 16, 1996, CNN reported testimony heard by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee about Russian organized crime in the United States. Former Mafia capo Michael Franzese told senators that Russian mob members were working with the Italian Mafia and using the United States as a base. CNN quoted him describing large cash payments and reported that he alleged Russian mob members devised gasoline-tax fraud schemes. The article also reported that Anthony “Gas Pipe” Casso, testifying behind a screen, said he had ordered a murder to protect a criminal racket; that is an allegation attributed to his testimony. CNN added that Drug Enforcement Administration officials told the hearing Russian and Italian groups were moving into drug deals. This is a report about general organized-crime testimony, not a committee finding about the Semion Mogilevich Organization. The accessible article does not mention Mogilevich or Donald Trump. TrumpFile’s separate page asserts that the hearing recognized Mogilevich’s organization and links the story to Trump through associates, but the cited Senate PDF could not be text-extracted in this review, and those assertions are not independently established here. The narrower event has no demonstrated Trump action or relationship, so it should be considered for exclusion from a Trump-event collection.
