children.title: Lutnick’s Newmark Divestiture Followed His Ethics Agreement
children.description_short: Howard Lutnick began selling Newmark holdings under an ethics agreement in May 2025 and completed the divestiture in October.
children.description_medium: Newmark’s SEC filing says Howard Lutnick agreed on May 16, 2025, to sell company shares as part of divestment required under his ethics agreement. It reports initial closings in May and completion on October 6. The filing identifies ethics compliance as the purpose; it does not establish a connection to tariff information.
children.description_long: Newmark Group’s annual filing to the SEC reports that Howard Lutnick agreed on May 16, 2025, to sell 10,969,533 Newmark Class A shares he beneficially owned. The filing says the first closing, for 10,839,674 shares held by Lutnick, his spouse and trusts, occurred May 19; a further 129,859 retirement-account shares were tied to later regulatory closing conditions. It states these transactions were pursuant to Lutnick’s agreement to divest company interests to comply with U.S. government ethics rules connected to his appointment as Commerce secretary. Newmark then reported that he completed his divestiture on October 6 and no longer had voting or dispositive power over the company’s securities. This is a separate ethics-agreement divestiture, distinct from Pete Hegseth’s March 24 transaction report. The filing does not connect Lutnick’s sales to tariff information or suggest they were pre-announcement trades. The record therefore describes a disclosed compliance process and does not treat the divestitures as evidence of opportunistic trading.

source_fact_map.quote: On May 16, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Board, agreed to sell to the Company 10,969,533 shares of Newmark Class A common stock beneficially owned by him
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: On May 16, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Board, agreed to sell to the Company 10,969,533 shares of Newmark Class A common stock beneficially owned by him, including (i) 7,989,936 shares held directly by Mr. Lutnick, (ii) 2,843,781 shares held in Mr. Lutnick’s personal asset trust, (iii) 3,384 shares held by the Mr. Howard Lutnick Family Trust, (iv) 2,573 shares held by Mr. Lutnick’s spouse, and (v) 129,859 shares originating from retirement accounts, including certain shares held by Mr. Lutnick’s spouse. The closing of the sale of the 10,839,674 shares held by him, his spouse, and the trusts occurred on May 19, 2025, and the closing of the sale of 129,859 shares held in retirement accounts will occur immediately after the closing of the sale of the voting shares of CFGM by Mr. Lutnick, which are pending subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approvals. These transactions are pursuant to Mr. Howard Lutnick’s agreement to divest his interests in the Company to comply with U.S. government ethics rules in connection with his appointment as the U.S. Secretary of Commerce. On October 6, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Company’s Board, completed his previously announced divestiture of his holdings in the Company in connection with his appointment as the U.S. Secretary of Commerce. Mr. Howard Lutnick no longer has any voting or dispositive power over any of the securities of the Company.

children.title: Trump Declares a National Emergency at the Southern Border
children.description_short: A January 20, 2025 proclamation declared a southern-border emergency and directed military support for border operations.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation declaring a national emergency at the U.S. southern border. The text invokes emergency and military authorities and directs the Defense Department to support Homeland Security with personnel, logistics, and additional barriers. It records the administration’s stated actions, not proof that each measure was implemented or that the proclamation’s factual assertions were accurate.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation declaring a national emergency at the U.S. southern border. The text invokes sections of the National Emergencies Act and makes military authorities available, including provisions under Title 10, sections 12302 and 2808. It directs the Department of Defense to support the Department of Homeland Security through personnel, detention space, transportation, logistics, and additional physical barriers. The proclamation states these measures are intended to help the federal government obtain operational control of the border. This entry records the declaration and its stated directives; the text alone does not show which measures were implemented or their effects. It also does not establish the accuracy of the proclamation’s claims about conditions at the border. The original held item incorrectly presented this as one omnibus emergency covering immigration, energy, and economic policy and asserted that it bypassed environmental, safety, and notice-and-comment requirements. The national energy emergency appears in a separate presidential action issued on the same date, and the supplied documents do not support the broader bypass claim.

source_fact_map.fact: Trump’s proclamation declares a national emergency at the southern border and invokes statutory emergency authority.

children.title: Trump Declares a National Energy Emergency
children.description_short: A separate January 20, 2025 order declared an energy emergency and directed agencies to use lawful authorities to advance domestic energy resources.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a separate order declaring a national energy emergency. The order cites asserted shortfalls in energy supply and directs agencies to identify and use lawful emergency and other authorities to facilitate domestic energy resources. The document establishes the declaration and its stated rationale, not the accuracy of its claims or the implementation and effects of its directives.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a separate executive order declaring a national energy emergency. The order cites asserted shortfalls in domestic energy production, transportation, refining, and generation and directs agencies to identify and exercise lawful emergency authorities, along with other lawful powers, to facilitate the identification, leasing, siting, production, transportation, refining, and generation of domestic energy resources. It describes energy supply and grid reliability as matters of economic and national security. This entry covers the specific energy action and its stated purpose; it does not verify the administration’s characterization of an energy emergency, show that every directed action was implemented, or quantify resulting changes to energy production, prices, or infrastructure. The original held item merged this order with a separate southern-border proclamation and characterized the combined action as bypassing environmental, safety, and notice-and-comment rules. The sources support two distinct declarations but do not substantiate that broad legal characterization. This copy therefore retains only what the energy order says and keeps its stated rationales attributed to the administration.

In light of these findings, I hereby declare a national emergency.

children.title: Trump DOJ Orders Review of FBI Personnel Tied to January 6 Cases Before Patel Takes Office
children.description_short: On Jan. 31, 2025, DOJ ordered a review of personnel tied to Jan. 6 cases, before Kash Patel became FBI director.
children.description_medium: On January 31, 2025, Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed federal prosecutors to list employees who worked on the January 6 Capitol investigation, while FBI officials tied to those cases faced personnel actions. The report described Patel as the nominee to lead the FBI, not its director. It does not substantiate a claim that Patel fired hundreds of agents for disloyalty.
children.description_long: On January 31, 2025, the Trump administration began a round of Justice Department and FBI personnel actions focused in part on staff who had worked on investigations related to the January 6 attack. Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove told federal prosecutors to compile a list of prosecutors and FBI agents who participated in the Capitol investigation. The same report said a memo ordered eight FBI officials to resign or face dismissal because of their work on January 6 cases, and separately described about 20 probationary prosecutors fired under a Bove order. Reuters also reported that the FBI Agents Association warned potentially hundreds of agents could be affected; that was a warning about possible scale, not a reported count of agents already fired. Kash Patel was still the nominee to direct the bureau and had appeared at a confirmation hearing the day before. This episode therefore belongs to Trump administration and Justice Department actions before Patel became FBI director. The reporting supports a personnel review and identified removals, but does not establish that Patel fired hundreds of agents for insufficient loyalty.

children.title: FBI Forces Out at Least Three Senior Officials, Including Brian Driscoll
children.description_short: The FBI forced out at least three senior officials in August 2025, including former acting director Brian Driscoll.
children.description_medium: The Washington Post reported that the FBI forced out at least three senior officials during a period of conflict with the Trump administration. One was former acting director Brian Driscoll, who had resisted demands to identify agents involved in January 6 investigations. The report places these departures during Kash Patel’s tenure, but does not say every official was dismissed for the same reason.
children.description_long: On August 7, 2025, The Washington Post reported that the FBI had forced out at least three senior officials who had clashed with the Trump administration. One was Brian Driscoll, the bureau’s former acting director during the first weeks of Trump’s second term. The report said Driscoll was fired by senior leaders and would finish his last day on Friday, August 8; the people quoted said he was given no reason for the firing. During his brief time leading the bureau, Driscoll had resisted demands from Trump Justice Department appointees to identify agents who worked on January 6 investigations. The article said he later provided the department a list of more than 5,000 FBI personnel identified only by employee identification number. It placed the departures during Kash Patel’s tenure. This is a distinct August personnel episode from the January 2025 review and the February 2026 agent dismissals. The source does not establish that all three officials worked on January 6 cases, that the same decisionmaker fired each one, or that a formal written rationale was issued. It documents reported departures amid a wider dispute over the treatment of bureau personnel.

children.title: FBI Fires at Least a Dozen Agents Tied to Trump Classified-Documents Probe
children.description_short: The FBI fired at least a dozen staff tied to Trump’s classified-documents probe in February 2026, The Washington Post reported.
children.description_medium: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country who were tied to the probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after he left office in 2021. This is a separate Patel-era episode; the report does not support the original claim that hundreds were fired for insufficient loyalty.
children.description_long: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country during that week. The article connected those employees to the FBI probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after leaving office in 2021. It described the dismissals as a continuation of Patel’s purge of bureau employees. This is a separate, later episode from the January 2025 review directed by acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove and the August 2025 departures of senior FBI officials. The available report supports the number “at least a dozen” for this specific week and describes the employees as tied to the classified-documents investigation. It does not establish that hundreds of agents were dismissed, that every affected employee was deemed insufficiently loyal, or that the February 2026 dismissals included employees tied to the separate 2020-election investigation. The original combined entry blended these episodes and attributed the January review to Patel before he led the bureau. This card preserves the Washington Post’s reported connection and allegation wording without turning the report into an independent finding about each employee or the president.

terminal_record.title: Justice Department Seeks to Terminate Flores Protections for Detained Children
terminal_record.description_short: Justice Department Seeks to Terminate Flores Protections for Detained Children
terminal_record.description_medium: On May 22, 2025, the Justice Department, DHS, and HHS filed a motion asking a federal court to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve an injunction covering agency regulations. The agreement sets protections for minors in immigration custody, including limits on detention and basic care standards. A federal judge denied the termination request in August, so the protections were not ended by this motion.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 22, 2025, the Justice Department, acting with the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services, asked a federal court to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve an injunction covering agency regulations. The 1997 agreement sets protections for children in immigration custody, including limits on detention and requirements for adequate food, water, and clean clothes. The filing argued that changed circumstances and agency regulations made continuation inequitable; that was the government’s position, not a court finding. The motion sought to end the settlement’s protections, but the request was not itself an effective termination. In August 2025, the district court denied the motion, saying the defendants had not identified new facts or law that warranted ending the agreement. This repaired entry records the government’s attempt to terminate court-supervised protections, with the correct May filing date and the distinction between a request and an enacted change. The February claim that the administration had already rescinded multiple agreements or eliminated independent oversight is not supported by these records. The later denial confirms that the Flores agreement remained in effect after this motion.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
U.S. District Court for the Central District of California

source_fact_map.fact: The Flores agreement limits detention time for children and requires basic care including adequate food, water, and clean clothes.
source_fact_map.quote: limit the amount of time children can be detained by immigration officials
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
The protections, which are drawn from a 1997 consent decree known as the Flores Settlement Agreement, limit the amount of time children can be detained by immigration officials. It also requires the government to provide children in its custody with adequate food, water and clean clothes.

The administration’s move to terminate the Flores agreement was long anticipated. In a court motion filed Thursday, the justice department argued that the Flores agreement should be “completely” terminated.

children.description_short: USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee report and set a target to publish final guidelines before the statutory deadline.
children.description_medium: USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee’s scientific report on March 11, 2025. The report was advisory, not the final guidelines; officials said they aimed to publish by the statutory deadline. Contemporaneous reporting described the committee’s evidence review and said it made no recommendation on ultra-processed foods.
children.description_long: On March 11, 2025, USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee’s scientific report. The committee’s report was an advisory document submitted to the departments; it was not the final federal Dietary Guidelines. USDA and HHS said they aimed to release the 2025–2030 guidelines before the statutory December 31 deadline and described future process improvements on transparency and conflicts of interest. Agri-Pulse reported that the committee spent 22 months reviewing nutrition evidence and that its recommendations included dietary-pattern advice. It also reported that the committee made no recommendation on ultra-processed foods, citing a lack of research. The sourced event is the agencies’ announcement of a review and timetable. The release’s political-science rhetoric does not establish that scientific conclusions were changed for political reasons. This card covers only the review announcement. The frozen parent also mixed in separate budget, CDC, grant, citation, local-food funding, and NIH personnel claims; those are not established by these sources and are not included here.

children.title: NIH Nutrition Researcher Kevin Hall Announces Early Retirement and Alleges Censorship
children.description_short: NIH researcher Kevin Hall announced early retirement and alleged HHS aides censored his work; HHS denied the accusation.
children.description_medium: NIH nutrition researcher Kevin Hall announced an early retirement on April 16, 2025, after 21 years. CBS News reported Hall’s allegations that HHS officials restricted interviews and other research communications. HHS denied censorship and disputed his account. The reports document competing statements, not a finding that officials censored Hall or caused his departure.
children.description_long: On April 16, 2025, NIH nutrition researcher Kevin Hall announced early retirement after 21 years at the agency. CBS News reported that Hall said he was stepping down and accused senior aides to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. of censorship. Hall told CBS that officials blocked a direct interview with a New York Times reporter about his ultra-processed-food research; he also said he was barred from presenting at a conference and faced demanded edits to a manuscript. These are Hall’s reported allegations. HHS denied editing his answers and rejected the censorship charge, saying NIH scientists could discuss research through written responses or other means and that it remained committed to gold-standard research. The Washington Post likewise described Hall’s concerns about political interference at NIH. The available sources establish the retirement announcement and competing accounts, not a factual finding that censorship occurred or that any specific official caused Hall to leave. The dietary-guidelines review is a separate event and is not part of this record.

terminal_record.title: Trump Allies Circulate Draft Election Emergency Order; Trump Says He Is Not Considering It
terminal_record.description_short: PBS reported a 17-page draft order among Trump allies proposed emergency powers over the 2026 midterms; Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency.
terminal_record.description_medium: PBS News reported on February 27, 2026, that a 17-page draft executive order circulating among Trump allies proposed declaring a national emergency to expand federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm elections. The draft included hand-counting and voter-identification provisions. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency around the midterms. The source describes a proposal, not an order Trump enacted.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 27, 2026, PBS News reported that a 17-page draft executive order was circulating among Trump allies. PBS said it reviewed the working document. The draft proposed declaring a national emergency and using it to assert federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm election process. Provisions described by PBS included hand-counted ballots, voter identification, and voter re-registration with proof of citizenship. The article presented these as elements of a proposal, not as changes that had taken effect. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring a national emergency around the midterms; in his reported response to a question about the draft, he said, “Who told you that?” Peter Ticktin, a Trump ally, confirmed to PBS that the draft had circulated among some supporters. The record therefore concerns circulation of a draft by allies and public reporting about Trump’s response. It does not establish that Trump ordered the draft, adopted it, deployed National Guard troops at polling places, or changed election administration under it. This entry makes no claim that the draft was enacted or implemented.

children.title: Israel Begins Strikes on Iran’s Nuclear and Military Sites
children.description_short: Israel began strikes against Iranian nuclear and military sites on June 13, 2025, including reported damage to underground structures at Natanz.
children.description_medium: On June 13, 2025, Israel began a strike campaign against Iranian nuclear facilities and military sites. Al Jazeera reported an initial Friday-morning wave and a separate later attack on Tabriz; it also attributed reported damage at Natanz to Israel’s military and described damage to residential buildings. This entry covers Israel’s opening action. U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear sites on June 21–22 in a separate operation, recorded in another child.
children.description_long: Israel began strikes on Iran on June 13, 2025, targeting nuclear facilities and military sites, according to Al Jazeera’s contemporaneous report. The report described an initial wave early Friday and a later, separate strike on Tabriz. It said Israel’s military claimed that its attacks damaged underground structures at the Natanz uranium-enrichment site and struck missile infrastructure; the Iranian Atomic Energy Organization said radioactive contamination from the Natanz strike remained within the site. The article also described damage to residential buildings, while casualty figures attributed to Iranian state media were presented as unofficial estimates and are not repeated here. The supplied record incorrectly combined this Israeli campaign with a later U.S. operation. U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear sites on June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, a separate action recorded in another child. This entry does not describe the two operations as coordinated or jointly executed, and it omits claims about congressional notification and War Powers violations that the accessed source does not establish.

children.title: United States Strikes Iranian Nuclear Sites in Operation Midnight Hammer
children.description_short: U.S. forces struck Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan in an operation spanning June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear facilities in Operation Midnight Hammer. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour on June 22, reported that B-2 bombers attacked Fordow and Natanz while submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles hit targets including Isfahan. The first bomber’s strike occurred at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, so the operation crossed a local-date boundary. U.S. officials’ damage claims and Iran’s denial are kept distinct.
children.description_long: On June 21–22, 2025, U.S. forces launched Operation Midnight Hammer against Iranian nuclear facilities. An Associated Press report published by PBS NewsHour described B-2 stealth bombers dropping bunker-buster bombs on the underground Fordow and Natanz enrichment sites and submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles striking targets including Isfahan. The report placed the first bomber’s strike at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, explaining why some accounts date the operation June 21 and others June 22. U.S. officials described the attack as devastating Iran’s nuclear program, but the same report said assessments were ongoing and Iran denied significant damage. The entry therefore records the strikes and weapons reported, not a settled conclusion about the program’s condition. The U.S. operation followed nine days of Israeli attacks, according to AP, but it was a distinct action. The original card’s claim that both countries conducted one coordinated operation beginning June 13 is not supported by these sources. Claims about congressional notification and a War Powers Act violation are also omitted because the accessed report does not establish them.

terminal_record.title: White House Terminates Some U.S. Attorneys in February 2025
terminal_record.description_short: NBC reported the White House terminated as many as a dozen U.S. attorneys on February 12, 2025; the reported total was not established.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 12, 2025, the White House terminated some U.S. attorneys during a wider change in federal prosecutorial leadership. NBC News reported terminations of as many as a dozen and said the precise total was not immediately available. Its account described immediate White House dismissals as a departure from the usual practice of Justice Department resignation requests.
terminal_record.description_long: On the evening of February 12, 2025, the White House terminated some U.S. attorneys during a transition in federal prosecutorial leadership. NBC News reported that the removals may have affected as many as a dozen offices and said its review found twelve names changed from a list published two days earlier. The Justice Department had not provided a total for how many of the nation’s 93 U.S. attorneys were affected. The article also noted that remaining Biden-nominated, Senate-confirmed attorneys were expected to leave, while immediate White House terminations departed from the usual practice of Justice Department resignation requests. This narrows the stored claim that all 93 attorneys were fired on January 20: the accessed reporting places terminations three weeks later and describes a limited number, not a complete one-day purge. It does not establish that all displaced attorneys were replaced by loyalists, that offices’ pending cases were left in limbo, or that prosecutors’ work was thereafter filtered through political loyalty. NBC reported that officials had not provided a final count. The account describes a personnel action and its reported departure from customary transitions, without asserting a legal finding about its propriety.
terminal_record.date_basis: The NBC article is dated February 13, 2025 and identifies the terminations as occurring Wednesday evening.

terminal_record.title: DOJ Drops Proposed Google AI-Investment Divestiture While Seeking Other Remedies
terminal_record.description_short: DOJ revised its Google search-case proposal on March 7, 2025, dropping mandatory AI-investment divestiture while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposed judgment in the Google search-monopoly case. The proposal dropped mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments in favor of advance notice for future investments, while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture and other remedies. Reuters reported that DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued seeking court relief. This was a change in proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case or a final court order.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice and plaintiff states filed a revised proposed final judgment in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. The filing changed the remedies sought: plaintiffs stopped seeking mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments and instead proposed prior notification of future investments. It maintained other central requests, including Google's divestiture of Chrome, restrictions on search-related payments to distribution partners, and data-sharing provisions. Reuters reported that DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Chrome's sale and other measures. The filing was a proposal submitted for the court's consideration; it did not dismiss the antitrust case or establish a quid pro quo. The supplied record's claim that Attorney General Pam Bondi dropped the case after Alphabet made political contributions or held meetings with Donald Trump is not supported by the accessed sources and is excluded. The official filing says plaintiffs changed the AI remedy after additional discovery, but this alone does not prove the rationale or rule out other motives. This corrected entry is limited to the documented procedural change and the remedies still proposed at that point.

children.title: Interior Orders Review to Unleash American Energy
children.description_short: Interior directed agencies to review rules and practices that could constrain domestic energy production.
children.description_medium: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced six new Secretary’s Orders, including Order 3418. The Department said it would encourage energy production on federal lands and review agency actions that could burden domestic energy development. The documented action is a policy direction; the sources do not establish resulting drilling or environmental effects.
children.description_long: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that he had signed six Secretary’s Orders on his first day in office. The Department described Secretary’s Order 3418, “Unleashing American Energy,” as aligning Interior with the president’s energy policy, encouraging energy exploration and production on federal lands and waters, and requiring review of agency actions that could burden domestic energy-resource development. The order also directed review of certain appropriations. This card records the policy direction and review instructions, not a measured change in drilling, leasing outcomes, or environmental conditions. The original entry’s Wyoming acreage and migration-corridor claims concern later lease events and are separated into another child. No 28-day permitting guarantee, acreage figure, or migration-corridor effect is carried into this copy because the accessed evidence for the February order does not establish those claims. The record identifies a federal policy direction with nationwide reach across Interior; operational effects and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

children.title: BLM Leases 114,439 Acres in June 2026 Wyoming Oil and Gas Sale
children.description_short: BLM offered 114,439 acres in Wyoming leases; the packet reports a sale, not drilling or production.
children.description_medium: On June 9, 2026, BLM reported leasing 102 Wyoming parcels totaling about 114,439 acres for $34.7 million in receipts. Its earlier notice had proposed 108 parcels and 119,595 acres. The sources establish a completed lease sale, not actual drilling or wildlife effects; leasing is only the first step before separate permit review.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2026, the Bureau of Land Management reported that it leased 102 Wyoming parcels totaling approximately 114,439 acres in a quarterly oil and gas sale, with $34,706,638 in total receipts. In March, the agency had announced 108 parcels totaling 119,595 acres for a planned June sale, so the final sale did not match the earlier offered-parcel total in the held entry. BLM states that leasing is the first step in federal oil and gas development and that an operator must submit an application for a permit to drill before development can begin. The supplied claim that the sale covered 250,000 acres near Yellowstone and Grand Teton or overlapped named wildlife migration corridors is not supported by the accessed sale notices and is omitted. These sources document leases and receipts, not actual drilling, production, emissions, or specific wildlife effects. The receipt total is reported by BLM and is not treated here as long-term government revenue or private profit. The event is a completed lease sale; later development and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

terminal_record.title: Tankers Turn Away and Pause Near Hormuz After U.S. Strikes on Iran
terminal_record.description_short: Tankers Turn Away and Pause Near Hormuz After U.S. Strikes on Iran
terminal_record.description_medium: On June 23, 2025, Reuters reported that at least two supertankers turned away near the Strait of Hormuz after U.S. strikes on Iran, while other ships paused or altered routes amid fears of a possible Iranian closure. Iran’s parliament had approved a closure measure, but it still required Supreme National Security Council approval; Reuters said Iran had never closed the strait. The report documents precautionary diversions, not a multi-day closure or a 40% oil-price spike.
terminal_record.description_long: Reuters reporting dated June 23, 2025, described changes in tanker routes after U.S. military strikes on Iran. Ship-tracking data showed at least two supertankers made U-turns near the Strait of Hormuz; several other vessels altered course or anchored outside the route. The report said the U.S. decision to join Israel’s attacks had increased fears of retaliation that might close the strait, through which about 20% of global oil and gas demand flows. It noted Iran’s parliament had approved a measure to close the waterway, but that it still required approval from the Supreme National Security Council; Reuters added that Iran had threatened closure before but never done so. The verified event is heightened shipping risk and precautionary vessel diversions. The available report does not substantiate a multi-day Iranian closure or the frozen record’s claim that global oil prices spiked more than 40% because of one. It also reports no completed closure or measured supply interruption.

terminal_record.title: Bondi DOJ Working Group Ordered Review of Federal Actions Involving Alvin Bragg
terminal_record.description_short: A February 2025 DOJ memo directed a working-group review that included alleged federal cooperation with Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi created the DOJ Weaponization Working Group and directed it to review federal enforcement activity from the previous four years. The memo included alleged federal cooperation with Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution among the subjects for review. It did not establish that allegation, announce a Bragg-specific criminal investigation, or find that Bragg acted improperly.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo establishing the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group. The directive assigned the group a review of federal civil and criminal enforcement activities during the previous four years and called for quarterly progress reports to the White House. Its list of topics included what the memo called “federal cooperation with the weaponization” by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, New York Attorney General Letitia James, their staffs, and other New York officials against Donald Trump and his businesses. That language states the administration’s allegation and the subject of a review; it is not a finding that Bragg coordinated with federal authorities or acted unlawfully. The memo also does not announce a criminal investigation into Bragg. The frozen entry’s claim that DOJ opened a February investigation into Bragg, along with its assertions about Bragg’s cooperation and a coordinated campaign against prosecutors, is not supported by the material reviewed and is omitted. The documented event is the DOJ review directive concerning the earlier Trump prosecutions.

terminal_record.title: Supreme Court Remands Bannon Case for Further Consideration
terminal_record.description_short: The Supreme Court vacated the judgment under review in Bannon’s case and remanded it in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment.
terminal_record.description_medium: On April 6, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court granted Steve Bannon’s petition, vacated the D.C. Circuit judgment, and remanded the case for further consideration in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment. The docket records a remand; it does not say the indictment was dismissed or that the conviction was set aside.
terminal_record.description_long: On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court granted Steve Bannon’s petition, vacated the judgment under review, and remanded the case for further consideration in light of a pending motion to dismiss the indictment. The Court’s docket identifies the lower court as the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and records that its decision was dated May 10, 2024, with rehearing denied on May 27, 2025. The Supreme Court docket later records that judgment issued on May 8, 2026. These entries describe the case’s path through appellate review and its return for further consideration. They do not show that the district court granted the motion to dismiss, that the indictment was dismissed, or that Bannon’s conviction was overturned. The action is a procedural remand, not a finding that the underlying prosecution was unlawful. The original entry joined this criminal case to a separate civil presidential-records lawsuit and alleged a broader dismantling of accountability; the docket does not support that connection. This account therefore confines itself to the Court’s recorded action and its stated basis.
organization_tags: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

terminal_record.title: Khamenei Rejects Trump’s Surrender Demand and Warns Against U.S. Intervention
terminal_record.description_short: Khamenei rejected Trump’s surrender demand and warned of damage if the U.S. entered the conflict.
terminal_record.description_medium: An Associated Press report published by PBS on June 18, 2025, said Ayatollah Ali Khamenei rejected President Donald Trump’s call for Iran’s unconditional surrender and warned that U.S. military involvement would cause “irreparable damage.” The report says Khamenei delivered the remarks in recorded video during Israeli strikes. This corrected draft omits the unsupported “gates of hell” and “severe and unrelenting” quotations.
terminal_record.description_long: On June 18, 2025, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for Iran’s unconditional surrender and warned that any U.S. military involvement would cause “irreparable damage,” according to an Associated Press report carried by PBS News. The report says Khamenei made the remarks in a recorded video aired by Iranian state television as Israeli strikes continued. It describes the address as Khamenei’s second public appearance since the strikes began and notes that Trump’s surrender demand came the previous day. This account corrects the frozen card’s June 15 date and narrows its claims to the remarks supported by the accessed report. The source does not support attributing “gates of hell” or a vow of “severe and unrelenting” revenge to Khamenei; those phrases are removed. Search results located “gates of hell” wording attributed to other Iranian figures, so that language is not reassigned to Khamenei. The reporting supports his rejection of the surrender demand and his conditional warning about U.S. military intervention. It does not establish the frozen card’s claims about proxy forces, global travel alerts, embassy closures, or a U.S. strike already having occurred before these June 18 remarks.

terminal_record.source_record_title: USPS Mail Consolidations and Trump EO Create Ballot Delivery Crisis Before 2026 Midterms
terminal_record.split_rationale: The supplied record combines a USPS postmark clarification and a distinct presidential executive order. Sources support two separately dated developments, but do not support a single nationwide ballot-delivery crisis or the claimed causal connection between USPS operations and ballot rejection counts.

children.title: USPS Clarifies How Machine Postmarks Record Postal Possession
children.description_short: USPS clarified that processing-facility postmarks may be later than first postal possession; the revision did not change existing postmarking practices.
children.description_medium: The Postal Service’s postmark revision, effective December 24, 2025, explained that a processing-facility postmark reflects the first automated processing date, which may follow initial postal possession. USPS said the text did not change existing operations and described manual counter postmarks that can match the mailing date. It did not establish late-ballot counts or ballot-rejection effects.
children.description_long: USPS’s Domestic Mail Manual revision concerning postmarks and postal possession took effect on December 24, 2025. The Postal Bulletin says the added section defined qualifying postmarks, described when they are applied, and explained how customers can obtain evidence of the date USPS accepted mail. It expressly says the wording did not change existing postal operations or postmarking practices. Under the stated standard, an automated processing-facility postmark shows the date of the first automated processing operation; that date may be later than the date USPS first took possession. USPS separately said transportation adjustments meant some mailpieces might not reach their originating processing facility on the day they were mailed. A customer presenting mail at a retail counter could request a manual local postmark aligning with the date of acceptance, and USPS said the guidance also applied to mail-in ballots. These sources support a description of the clarification and disclosed operating context. They do not establish a count of late ballots, a particular election’s rejection total, or that the rule caused a voter’s ballot to arrive late. The materials also do not attribute this USPS action to Trump. This child records that bounded postal development without repeating the combined card’s unsupported claim of a nationwide ballot-delivery crisis.

Manual postmarks will be applied free of charge. This guidance is the same for all types of mailpieces, including mail-in ballots.

children.title: Trump Signs EO 14399 Directing USPS to Propose Mail-Ballot Standards
children.description_short: Trump’s March 2026 election order directed USPS to propose ballot-mail standards; it did not itself enact a ballot-refusal rule.
children.description_medium: Trump signed EO 14399 on March 31, 2026, directing USPS to propose mail-in ballot service standards and DHS to compile state citizenship lists. It called for proposed envelope markings and barcodes; it did not itself enact ballot-refusal rules. California DOJ reported key provisions remained blocked in plaintiff states during appeal.
children.description_long: On March 31, 2026, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14399, titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.” Among other directions, the order told the Postmaster General to start a proposed rulemaking within 60 days for USPS mail-in and absentee ballot services. The notice was to include proposed requirements such as an Official Election Mail marking and a unique Intelligent Mail barcode on outbound ballot mail. The same order directed the Department of Homeland Security, with Social Security Administration coordination, to compile and transmit state citizenship lists to chief election officials. These passages show a signed executive order directing a rulemaking process; they do not show that USPS had already adopted a rule refusing to carry ballots based on a federal voter list. In July 2026, California’s Attorney General reported that the First Circuit left a district court order blocking key provisions in place for the plaintiff States while the appeal proceeded, including the USPS ballot restriction and DHS eligibility lists. That is a party’s public account of the court posture, scoped to those states and that period. No fact in the source packet establishes that the order caused a nationwide ballot-delivery crisis, the stored California rejection count, or the alleged local advice to abandon mail voting. This child therefore describes the enacted order and proposed USPS action separately from implementation, litigation, and broader effects.

terminal_record.description_short: Trump’s June 21 Truth Social post said U.S. forces had attacked three Iranian nuclear sites and called for peace.
terminal_record.description_medium: An archive of Donald Trump’s June 21, 2025 Truth Social posts records a message saying the United States had completed an attack on three Iranian nuclear sites and naming Fordow, Natanz and Esfahan. He wrote, “NOW IS THE TIME FOR PEACE!” The archived post does not contain the supplied title’s phrase “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED IRAN!” This correction records Trump’s published words without treating his success claim as an independent damage assessment.
terminal_record.description_long: On June 21, 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the United States had completed an attack on three Iranian nuclear sites. The archived post names Fordow, Natanz and Esfahan, says the aircraft had left Iranian airspace, and calls for peace. This is the wording preserved in the American Presidency Project’s dated archive of Trump’s Truth Social posts. The supplied record’s title attributed the phrase “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED IRAN!” to him, but that wording does not appear in the June 21 post reviewed here. The corrected copy therefore describes the contemporaneous message without putting that phrase in Trump’s mouth. Trump characterized the military operation as successful; the post does not independently establish the amount of damage or the status of Iran’s nuclear program. PolitiFact’s subsequent review quoted military experts saying it was too soon to know whether the sites had been completely destroyed. The event captured here is Trump’s public announcement and its stated call for peace, not a finding about the operation’s effectiveness or the later course of the conflict.

children.title: Paramount Settles Trump’s 60 Minutes Lawsuit for $16 Million
children.description_short: Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview; the settlement did not establish that the interview was improperly edited.
children.description_medium: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Donald Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. PBS NewsHour reported that Trump alleged the interview was edited to improve how Harris sounded, which CBS denied. Paramount said the money would go to Trump’s future presidential library and that CBS would not issue an apology. PBS also reported that Paramount was seeking merger approval from the Trump administration; concerns about a connection were reported as allegations, not proven as an exchange.
children.description_long: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay Donald Trump $16 million to settle his lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump alleged that the interview had been edited to improve how Harris sounded; CBS denied the allegation. Paramount said the payment would go to the president’s future library and that the settlement did not require an apology. The case therefore ended in a payment, not a court finding that CBS had manipulated the interview. PBS NewsHour’s report also described a separate context: Paramount was seeking administration approval for its proposed Skydance merger, and interview guest Brian Stelter said that was why the word “bribe” had come up in public discussion. Paramount and the FCC denied that suggestion. The reporting does not establish that merger review was exchanged for the settlement or that the administration conditioned approval on payment. This entry records the settlement and the attributed concern without treating coercion as a proven fact. Other incidents in the original card are handled separately.

children.description_short: Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $1.1 billion allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a bill canceling about $9 billion in previously approved foreign-aid and public-broadcasting spending. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour, said about $1.1 billion was allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which finances NPR and PBS, with most of that amount distributed to more than 1,500 local stations. children.description_long: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $9 billion in previously approved spending for public broadcasting and foreign aid. The Associated Press reported through PBS NewsHour that about $1.1 billion had been allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which financed NPR and PBS; most of that amount was distributed to more than 1,500 local public radio and television stations. The article describes a completed federal rescission, not merely a proposed cut. It says the White House had presented the bill as a test case for additional rescission packages and reports that Democrats unanimously opposed it but could not stop it. This card is limited to the signed rescission and the reported funding channel. It does not claim that the entire $1.1 billion would have gone directly to NPR or PBS, that every local station lost the same amount, or that specific station closures followed. The original record grouped this measure with separate legal disputes, media criticism, FCC inquiries, and immigration enforcement; those actions are not part of this dated entry.

children.title: White House Media Page Labels News Outlets as “Offenders”

children.description_medium: By December 3, 2025, the White House maintained a webpage labeling selected news coverage and outlets as media “offenders.” Reporters Without Borders described sections called “Media Offender of the Week,” “Hall of Shame,” and a leaderboard; it reported that CBS News, The Boston Globe, and The Independent appeared in the first section. terminal_record.title: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
terminal_record.description_short: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
terminal_record.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while programs were reviewed. Reuters reported that exemptions included $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza, while the Associated Press later reported that hundreds of millions in USAID payments to aid groups remained frozen and officials had no confirmed payments to Middle East partners. The evidence supports disruption, not a complete cutoff of all Palestinian aid.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while the administration reviewed whether programs aligned with its foreign-policy priorities. Reuters reported that the pause halted funding across assistance programs and later reviewed a list of exemptions, finding that only limited humanitarian relief was released. Among the approved exceptions were $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza. That limited carveout makes the frozen entry’s claim that all U.S. aid to Palestinians was eliminated inaccurate. The interruption still had reported effects: in March, the Associated Press reported that hundreds of millions of dollars in USAID contractual payments to aid groups were frozen, and that officials had no confirmed payments to partners in the Middle East after the January 31 Gaza waiver. The reporting distinguishes authorization from delivery: more than $383 million was approved for Gaza relief, while payment remained unconfirmed. The supported event is therefore a broad aid freeze that disrupted Gaza assistance despite exceptions, not a completed categorical cutoff of every Palestinian program. The cited reports do not establish the frozen entry’s annual aid total, a Foreign Assistance Act violation, or a specific administration rationale about Palestinians.

children.title: DOJ and FBI Say Their Epstein Review Found No Incriminating Client List
children.description_short: DOJ and FBI Say Their Epstein Review Found No Incriminating Client List
children.description_medium: On July 7, 2025, the Justice Department and FBI released a memorandum describing a review of investigative holdings relating to Jeffrey Epstein. The agencies said the review found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence to predicate an investigation of uncharged third parties. The memorandum says victim privacy and court seals limited disclosure.
children.description_long: The Justice Department and FBI’s July 7, 2025 memorandum described a review of investigative holdings relating to Jeffrey Epstein and the agencies’ decision about further disclosure. It said FBI personnel searched digital systems and physical storage locations, then had agents, analysts, attorneys, and privacy and civil-liberties experts review the material. The agencies said the files included images and videos involving minors and identifying information about victims; it also said much of the material was subject to court-ordered sealing. The memorandum stated that the review found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence that could predicate an investigation of uncharged third parties. It described Epstein as having harmed more than one thousand victims and said no further disclosure was appropriate or warranted. These are the government’s stated conclusions about its review; the memorandum does not say every person associated with Epstein was investigated or exonerated. This record covers the July review and its public findings alone. It does not treat the memo as proof of the separate birthday-message dispute or the later DOJ investigation request.

children.title: Trump Sues Wall Street Journal over Epstein Birthday-Note Report
children.description_short: Trump sued the Wall Street Journal over its report about a 2003 Epstein birthday greeting.
children.description_medium: Reuters reported that Trump filed a defamation suit on July 18, 2025, seeking at least $10 billion from the Wall Street Journal and related defendants over its report about a 2003 birthday greeting to Jeffrey Epstein. Trump denied the report, and Reuters said it had not verified the underlying account. The suit’s allegations were not a court finding.
children.description_long: Reuters reported that President Donald Trump filed a defamation suit on July 18, 2025, against the Wall Street Journal and its owners, including Rupert Murdoch, seeking at least $10 billion. The lawsuit followed the newspaper’s report that Trump’s name appeared on a 2003 birthday greeting for Jeffrey Epstein with a sexually suggestive drawing and a reference to secrets they shared. Reuters said the complaint alleged that the story defamed Trump and caused financial and reputational harm. Trump denied the Journal’s account, and Reuters stated that it had not independently verified the underlying report. This record treats the filing as a confirmed legal action and the birthday message as an allegation in reporting that Trump disputed. A complaint’s allegations do not establish defamation, and a reported denial does not resolve whether the message existed or who wrote it. The suit is a separate July event from the Justice Department and FBI’s review memorandum and from the later announcement that federal prosecutors would examine Epstein’s ties to political figures. This description does not imply any court ruling or final result in the case.

children.description_long: On November 14, 2025, Reuters reported that the Justice Department would fulfill President Donald Trump’s request to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s ties to former President Bill Clinton and JPMorgan. Attorney General Pam Bondi said Jay Clayton, the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, would lead the investigation. Reuters reported that Trump also asked the department to examine former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers and Reid Hoffman, and that all three men had been mentioned in documents released by the House Oversight Committee. The article said the department’s decision came despite a July memorandum in which DOJ and the FBI said they had found no evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties. Reuters characterized Trump as seeking to shift attention from his own relationship with Epstein and noted that the inquiry could face a challenge as vindictive prosecution; these are attributed reporting and analysis, not judicial findings. This record covers the request and announced assignment only. It does not say that charges were filed, that investigators reached conclusions, or that the named individuals committed wrongdoing.

children.title: Trump Vetoes Yemen War Powers Resolution
children.description_short: Trump vetoed S.J. Res. 7, a resolution concerning U.S. armed forces in hostilities in or affecting Yemen.
children.description_medium: On April 16, 2019, President Donald Trump vetoed S.J. Res. 7, a joint resolution concerning removal of U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in or affecting Yemen. In his message, Trump argued the measure would constrain his commander-in-chief authority and harm U.S. foreign policy. The archive records the veto and his stated rationale; it does not establish the resolution's effects on the conflict or civilian harm.
children.description_long:
On April 16, 2019, President Donald Trump returned S.J. Res. 7 without approval. The joint resolution sought to direct the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in or affecting Yemen, with exceptions. In the veto message, Trump argued that the United States was not engaged in hostilities in Yemen apart from counterterrorism operations against al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and ISIS. He also said the measure would interfere with his commander-in-chief authority and could harm U.S. foreign policy.

This record isolates the Yemen War Powers veto from the separate July arms-export vetoes. It presents the president's explanation as a position in the veto message, not as a neutral finding about the conflict or Congress's authority. The accessible archive establishes the veto message and its contents; it does not measure what followed from the veto, prove its effect on hostilities or establish downstream civilian harm. The message describes the resolution's exceptions only generally, so this draft does not supply additional statutory language.

children.description_medium: On July 24, 2019, Donald Trump vetoed three joint resolutions that would have blocked specified defense export licenses involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and European partners. His messages argued the restrictions would harm security cooperation and U.S. foreign relations. The official archive identifies each resolution and the proposed transfers; these records do not establish later transfer outcomes, monetary totals or a connection to Jamal Khashoggi.
children.description_long:
On July 24, 2019, President Donald Trump returned three joint resolutions without approval: S.J. Res. 36, 37 and 38. The measures addressed different export licenses and transfers. The archived messages describe components for Saudi Arabia's Paveway production in S.J. Res. 36, Paveway II kits for the United Arab Emirates and European partners in S.J. Res. 37, and the Aurora Fuzing System for the Paveway IV program involving Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom in S.J. Res. 38.

Trump argued that the proposed restrictions would weaken security partnerships, hurt U.S. foreign relations and undermine defense cooperation. In each message he also presented continued licensing as a way to support partners and, in his view, reduce civilian casualties in Yemen. Those are the President's stated reasons, not independent findings about the transfers or their effects. This record corrects the original April date and separates the arms vetoes from the Yemen War Powers veto. The archive does not establish the ultimate disposition of each license, the value of any transfer, a link to Khashoggi's murder or a measurable effect on civilians.

terminal_record.title: Unverified Claim: Federal Benefits for Same-Sex Spouses Restricted in February 2025
terminal_record.description_short: Unverified claim: federal agencies restricted benefits for same-sex spouses in February 2025.
terminal_record.description_medium: The supplied record alleges that federal agencies changed benefits rules in February 2025 to disadvantage same-sex married couples, affecting survivor benefits, federal employee health coverage, and spousal immigration rights. It includes no directive or contemporaneous report establishing those changes. SSA guidance covers only two Medicare procedures and does not resolve the broader allegation.
terminal_record.description_long: The supplied record alleges that the Trump administration changed federal benefits rules in February 2025 to disadvantage same-sex married couples, naming Social Security survivor benefits, federal employee health coverage, and spousal immigration rights. The packet includes no directive or contemporaneous report establishing those changes. It also says the marriages themselves remained legally recognized; no sourced material here establishes a change to that status. Social Security Administration guidance dated February 7, 2025 treats same-sex and opposite-sex marriages alike for two specific Medicare procedures: special enrollment eligibility and rollback of a premium surcharge. Those limited procedures do not determine whether survivor benefits, federal employee coverage, or immigration rules changed. The broad policy allegation therefore remains unverified, and the supplied materials do not establish which agency acted, what rule changed, when it took effect, or who was affected. No measured impact or outcome is documented.

children.title: Springfield Faces Threats and School Disruptions Amid False Pet-Eating Claims
children.description_short: Springfield Faces Threats and School Disruptions Amid False Pet-Eating Claims
children.description_medium: PBS NewsHour reported on September 17, 2024, that false claims about Haitian immigrants stealing and eating pets had been amplified by Donald Trump and JD Vance. Springfield officials told Reuters they had no credible reports supporting the claims. By the PBS report, the city had experienced threats, school closures, fear in the immigrant community, and a canceled festival; the report said no bombs or attacks had occurred.
children.description_long: PBS NewsHour’s September 17, 2024 report described Springfield after false claims about Haitian immigrants stealing or eating pets were amplified by Donald Trump and JD Vance. Reuters Fact Check reported the week earlier that the narrative surfaced online without credible evidence. Springfield police told Reuters there were no credible reports or specific claims of pets being harmed by members of the immigrant community. Reuters also documented that a Canton cat-killing case circulated online as support for the rumor involved a lifelong Canton resident who was not Haitian. By the NewsHour report, Springfield was dealing with multiple threats against city hall, schools, universities, and community centers. The reporter said no bombs had been found and no attacks had happened. City Manager Bryan Heck said pet-eating was not a problem, while bomb threats were. PBS reported that the city canceled its CultureFest partly because of the threats. This draft covers the rumor and the immediate Springfield response; it does not claim every threat came from the rumor or link it to a separate immigration policy.

children.title: Court Blocks DHS’s Planned September 2025 Haiti TPS Cutoff
children.description_short: Court Blocks DHS’s Planned September 2025 Haiti TPS Cutoff
children.description_medium: DHS’s July 1, 2025 Federal Register notice set a September 2 cutoff for Haiti’s TPS designation. A July 15 federal judgment stayed the earlier termination, making any cutoff no earlier than February 3, 2026; the September date did not take effect. USCIS later reported that a separate termination became effective July 27, 2026. This policy and court sequence is distinct from the Springfield rumor and from humanitarian parole.
children.description_long: On July 1, 2025, DHS published a notice that purported to terminate Haiti’s TPS designation at 11:59 p.m. local time on September 2. Reuters reported that the move concerned roughly half a million Haitian beneficiaries. On July 15, a federal court in Haitian Evangelical Clergy Association v. Trump entered judgment making any termination effective no earlier than February 3, 2026; Haitian beneficiaries retained TPS and work authorization through that date. The September 2025 cutoff therefore did not take effect. USCIS later reported that, following a separate 2026 decision, Haiti’s TPS designation terminated effective July 27, 2026. That later status does not mean the 2025 cutoff happened on time. This record documents the 2025 policy notice and its court-ordered delay, with later status supplied for clarity. No source supports a causal link between the Springfield rumor and the TPS decision. Temporary Protected Status is a statutory designation and should not be described as humanitarian parole.

terminal_record.title: Trump Revoked EO 11246 and Changed Federal Contractor DEI Rules
terminal_record.description_short: A Jan. 21 order revoked EO 11246, set a 90-day transition, and limited contractor certification to DEI programs that violate federal law.
terminal_record.description_medium: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump revoked Executive Order 11246, which governed equal-employment requirements for federal contractors. The order allowed contractors to continue under the January 20 regulatory scheme for 90 days during the transition. It directed agencies to require certification that a contractor does not operate DEI programs that violate federal anti-discrimination law; it did not require contractors to eliminate every DEI program.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the order “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity.” Section 3 revoked Executive Order 11246, the federal contractor equal-employment order, and allowed contractors to continue complying with the regulatory scheme in effect on January 20 for 90 days. It directed the Labor Department's Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to stop holding contractors responsible for affirmative action and related practices described in the order. The order also required agencies to add contract terms concerning compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws and certification that a contractor does not operate DEI programs that violate those laws. That language is narrower than the frozen entry's claim that all contractor DEI requirements ended immediately or that contractors had to eliminate all DEI programs. The order took effect as an executive directive on January 21, but the 90-day transition means the change was staged. This record describes the order and its text; it makes no claim about court outcomes or documented injuries to a specific contractor, employee, or protected group.

children.description_short: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged Fox News viewers to buy Tesla stock, prompting federal ethics questions.
children.description_medium: On March 19, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged Fox News viewers to buy Tesla stock. The Washington Post reported the recommendation the next day and described it as an apparent ethics-rule violation. CNBC quoted Lutnick’s on-air recommendation and summarized rules restricting federal employees from using their office to endorse businesses. children.description_long: On March 19, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appeared on Fox News and urged viewers to buy Tesla stock. The Washington Post reported the recommendation the next day and described it as an apparent violation of federal ethics rules that prohibit officials from endorsing products or businesses. CNBC quoted Lutnick saying, “If you want to learn something on this show tonight, buy Tesla,” and summarized the rule against using a government position or title to endorse a product, service or enterprise. The available reporting establishes the televised recommendation and why it raised ethics questions. It does not establish a formal finding that Lutnick violated the law, an enforcement action, or that the recommendation changed Tesla’s share price. The original combined record also attributed this advice to a wider pattern of cabinet self-dealing and tied it to broad claims about Lutnick’s holdings. Those separate claims are not included in this event card. The documented event is the public recommendation and the ethics concern it prompted; no conclusion about private gain is drawn here. The reviewed sources also do not establish whether Lutnick personally traded Tesla shares after the broadcast.

children.title: Scott Bessent Says He Divested His North Dakota Soybean-Farmland Interest
children.description_short: Scott Bessent said he sold his North Dakota soybean-farmland interest as part of his ethics agreement.
children.description_medium: On December 7, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had recently divested his North Dakota soybean-farmland interest under his ethics agreement. The Associated Press reported that the agreement required him to divest his portion of the investment. An August Office of Government Ethics letter described a December 15 target for remaining divestitures and confirmed recusals from matters affecting the assets. The record does not establish a specific farm-sale deadline or an ethics finding about this sale.
children.description_long: On December 7, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had recently divested his interest in North Dakota soybean farmland, describing the sale as part of his ethics agreement. The Associated Press reported his remarks on Face the Nation and said the agreement required divestment of his portion of the investment, which was held through a family partnership. Months earlier, the Office of Government Ethics told the Senate Finance Committee that Treasury officials expected remaining asset divestitures by December 15 because the assets were illiquid; the office also said Bessent was recused from particular matters affecting those assets. These sources document Bessent’s reported sale and the broader compliance process. They do not establish that this specific farm remained unsold for exactly eleven months, that a formal OGE notice specifically concerned the farm, or that Bessent acted on a matter affecting it while conflicted. The original card joined the divestiture to Lutnick’s Tesla recommendation, but the events occurred on different dates and concern different officials. This child card keeps the farm divestiture as a separate ethics event and does not characterize it as a finding of corruption or unlawful conduct.

terminal_record.title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Order Targeting the Minority Business Agency
terminal_record.description_short: EO 14238 directed MBDA to sharply reduce functions; a federal court later preliminarily enjoined implementation after staff and grant actions.
terminal_record.description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14238 on March 14, 2025, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory operations and staffing to the legal minimum. The Rhode Island federal court later recorded that most MBDA staff were placed on leave and grants appeared terminated, then granted a preliminary injunction. This account corrects the February date and does not claim all federal minority-business support ended.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14238, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions to the maximum extent allowed by law and reduce statutory work and staffing to the legal minimum. Afterward, MBDA placed all but five employees on paid administrative leave, and the district court said the agency appeared to have terminated its existing grants. In its May 6 preliminary order, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island stated that the executive order, as carried out, violated the Administrative Procedure Act in an arbitrary and capricious way and disregarded Congress’s role in authorizing agencies and appropriating funds. The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order at MBDA. That was a preliminary ruling, not a final merits judgment. The records do not show that all federal minority-business support or SBA programs ended, or establish later agency operations after the injunction.

children.title: Trump Dismisses NSA and Cyber Command Chief Timothy Haugh
children.description_short: Trump Dismisses NSA and Cyber Command Chief Timothy Haugh
children.description_medium: On April 3, 2025, President Donald Trump dismissed Gen. Timothy Haugh as director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command. NSA deputy Wendy Noble was also removed and reassigned. Reuters reported that Laura Loomer had urged Trump to dismiss Haugh and met with him the day before; officials cited in the reporting did not know the reason for the personnel decisions.
children.description_long: On April 3, 2025, President Donald Trump dismissed Gen. Timothy Haugh as director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command. NSA deputy director Wendy Noble was also removed from her post and reassigned within the Pentagon, according to Reuters. Reuters reported that Laura Loomer, an outside political activist, had urged Trump to dismiss Haugh and met with the president the day before the firing. The reporting does not establish that Loomer had formal authority over the personnel decision, and it does not confirm her accusation that Haugh was disloyal. Officials cited in the reporting said they did not know the reason for Haugh’s dismissal or Noble’s reassignment. The event documented here is the removal of senior leaders from the NSA and Cyber Command; Reuters also situated it within a broader round of White House national-security dismissals. This record does not claim that Loomer ordered the removals or that they caused a specific intelligence failure. It treats the later revocation of 37 intelligence clearances in August as a separate event because the sources describe a different date and decision process.

source_fact_map.fact: Trump dismissed Haugh as NSA director on April 3, and Haugh also headed U.S. Cyber Command; NSA deputy Wendy Noble was dismissed with him.
source_fact_map.quote: U.S. President Donald Trump fired General Timothy Haugh as director of the National Security Agency
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
WASHINGTON, April 3 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump fired General Timothy Haugh as director of the National Security Agency, in a national security purge that sources said on Friday included more than a dozen staff at the White House national security council.

NSA director Air Force General Haugh, who is also head of U.S. Cyber Command, was dismissed along with Wendy Noble, his deputy at the NSA, two sources familiar with the decision said.

Media outlets including The Washington Post had reported Haugh's firing on Thursday night, citing current and former U.S. officials, who said they did not know the reason for Haugh’s dismissal or Noble’s reassignment. Noble was reassigned to a job within the Pentagon.

Media outlets including The Washington Post had reported Haugh's firing on Thursday night, citing current and former U.S. officials, who said they did not know the reason for Haugh’s dismissal or Noble’s reassignment. Noble was reassigned to a job within the Pentagon.

children.description_short: Gabbard Revokes Clearances of 37 Intelligence Professionals
children.description_medium: On August 19, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard announced that she revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former intelligence professionals, accusing them of politicizing and manipulating intelligence. Reuters reported that Gabbard said she acted at President Donald Trump’s direction. Those accusations were the administration’s stated rationale, not findings about each person.
children.description_long: On August 19, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard announced that she had revoked security clearances held by 37 current and former intelligence professionals. Reuters reported that Gabbard accused them of “politicizing and manipulating intelligence” and said she acted at President Donald Trump’s direction. Those statements describe the administration’s stated rationale; the cited reporting does not establish the allegations as findings against each individual. The event documented here is the clearance revocation, not proof that each person mishandled intelligence or violated professional standards. Reuters’ account does not support the frozen entry’s specific descriptions of the CIA’s top Russia analyst or a 29-year veteran, so those details are omitted. The August decision is distinct from the April removal of NSA director Timothy Haugh and deputy Wendy Noble. Sources supplied for that earlier episode report Laura Loomer’s advocacy, but the August reporting does not link her to Gabbard’s action. This entry records the action and its stated justification without asserting an independent legal or factual determination.

terminal_record.description_medium: An internal, unverified draft about the supplied packet's account that Donald Trump named Michael Ellis CIA deputy director on February 3, 2025.
