terminal_record.description_long:
An internal draft isolates one action from a much broader original entry: the supplied packet says President Donald Trump named Michael Ellis as CIA deputy director on February 3, 2025. The packet describes Ellis as a lawyer and former aide to Representative Devin Nunes and says the deputy role does not require Senate confirmation. CIA's accessible announcement confirms that Ellis was sworn in as deputy director and lists prior service as NSA general counsel, senior director for intelligence programs at the National Security Council, House intelligence committee general counsel and a Navy Reserve intelligence officer.

Those details describe the role and career background; they do not, by themselves, establish when Trump selected him or prove the draft's political-loyalty characterization. The May National Intelligence Council personnel changes, March probationary dismissals and August clearance and Russia-specialist actions in the source packet concern separate events and are excluded from this entry. The source report about the selection timed out during access, so this remains an unverified supplied draft and is not cleared for publication.

The Boston Globe reported that he attacked the Affordable Care Act, promised “much better health care under a much better price,” and had yet to outline a specific plan. This supports a narrow description of the exchange and a promise, not an enacted program. The frozen synopsis’s scene of Trump holding a blank sheet at an October 15 rally is not supported by this contemporaneous account, which describes a town hall and no paper prop. Searches also surfaced later October reporting about a separate 60 Minutes interview and a healthcare-accomplishments binder; that later story does not establish the alleged October 15 rally scene and is not substituted here. This card preserves only the documented October 15 health-policy answer. The available report gives no coverage mechanism, cost estimate, bill, or subsequent outcome. It also does not establish whether Trump had a separate proposal elsewhere; the description is limited to his answer at this event.

terminal_record.title: Administration Temporarily Withholds 22 Title X Grants
terminal_record.description_short: On March 31, 2025, Title X grantees were notified that the administration would temporarily withhold funding for 22 grants beginning April 1.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funds for 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning care, including contraception. The Guttmacher Institute estimated that if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care over a year; that figure is conditional, not a count of confirmed losses.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funding from 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning services, including contraception, for low-income people. The Guttmacher Institute reported that all 13 direct grants to Planned Parenthood affiliates were included among the 22. It estimated that, if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care in a year. That estimate is conditional: it is not a count of people already deprived of care. The evidence supports a temporary, targeted withholding in April 2025. This card does not repeat the original assertions that all federal contraceptive support ended in February or that the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive coverage requirement was rescinded then; the cited record establishes the Title X grant action. The estimate and consequences remain attributed to Guttmacher, and the sources reviewed do not establish whether the withheld funds were later restored or how many patients lost services.

terminal_record.description_medium: An FBI proffer record from 2019 was reported to contain a redacted former assistant’s statement that Jeffrey Epstein introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump. The report says the interview occurred in July 2019 and that the document is dated November 2019. The statement is an allegation, not an established account of how the couple met; public accounts described different introductions. The record does not substantiate the original 209-file count.
terminal_record.description_long: In a 2019 FBI proffer, a redacted former assistant to Jeffrey Epstein said that Epstein introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump. The Daily Beast reported that the witness made the claim during a July 2019 interview with FBI agents and federal prosecutors, and quoted the heavily redacted record as stating that Epstein introduced Melania to Donald Trump. The underlying allegation remains unverified. The article noted that the claim conflicts with Melania Trump’s memoir and with Donald Trump’s account, and reported that the Justice Department had warned that the file release could contain false or falsely submitted material. The FBI document is dated November 2019, while the interview is reported as occurring in July 2019. This is a separate, related file record, not a correction of the frozen entry’s distinct 2002-email date; that email item is omitted because the accessed sources do not substantiate it. This draft therefore centers the reported contents of one proffer and omits the claim that Melania appears in 209 EFTA documents, because the supplied record cites no verifiable count for that number. It does not infer knowledge, participation, or wrongdoing from a witness statement.

terminal_record.title: DOJ Withdrew Eight OVW Grant Notices and Later Reopened Funding With New Terms
terminal_record.description_short: DOJ withdrew eight OVW grant notices in February 2025, then issued revised opportunities in May. The record documents a pause and reissue, not elimination of all OVW grants.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 6, 2025, the Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women removed eight listed grant opportunities and told applicants that the notices were under revision. The 19th reported no updated funding notices until May 7, after the original deadlines; three months later, six new opportunities appeared, only two corresponding to the withdrawn set. DOJ later announced 19 FY2025 notices. This was a pause and revised release, not the elimination of every OVW grant.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 6, 2025, the Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women removed eight grant opportunities listed on its website and replaced them with a notice that applications were under revision. Reporting by The 19th, republished by Rewire News Group, said the office posted no updated funding notices until May 7, after the original application deadlines. Three months after the February removal, six new grant opportunities appeared, and only two were among those originally taken down. On May 23, the DOJ announced that OVW had released 19 notices of funding opportunity for FY2025 grants addressing domestic and dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The revised notices included changed priorities and restrictions. These facts support a record about a temporary withdrawal, delay, and revised grant release. They contradict the frozen entry's claim that the administration eliminated every OVW grant program in February and terminated more than $500 million in annual OVW funding. The cited reporting describes uncertainty for applicants, but does not establish that all survivor services ended, that shelters turned people away, or that the entire annual OVW budget was terminated. The corrected account keeps the reported pause and reissue distinct from unrelated DOJ grant cancellations.

held_record.title: Trump Administration Interfering in 2026 Midterm Elections
held_record.synopsis: The Trump administration is interfering in the 2026 midterm elections to entrench the imperial presidency. The administration is effectuating a multipronged plan to subvert the elections and cement its power and policy agenda without accountability.

survivor_record.title: Trump Administration Interfering in 2026 Midterm Elections
survivor_record.synopsis: The Trump administration is interfering in the 2026 midterm elections in an effort to entrench the imperial presidency. The administration is using a multipronged plan to subvert the elections and cement its power and policy agenda without accountability.
survivor_record.description_medium: The Center for American Progress argued that the Trump administration was using several methods to influence the 2026 midterms. Its fact sheet lists efforts involving election-denier appointments, federal voter data, agency cuts and executive orders affecting voting access. These are CAP’s claims and framing, not court findings.
survivor_record.description_long: The Center for American Progress published a fact sheet on August 19, 2026, arguing that the Trump administration was using a multipronged strategy to shape the 2026 midterm elections. Its examples included public claims casting doubt on election integrity, appointments of election deniers to federal roles, cuts to agencies and election-security programs, demands for voter information from states, and executive orders aimed at voting procedures. The organization also warned about possible federal pressure on election certification. CAP presented these measures as a coordinated effort to consolidate power, so that interpretation should be attributed to the advocacy group rather than treated as an adjudicated finding. The fact sheet identifies concrete policy actions and proposals behind its concern, giving the record more substance than a general claim of interference. It does not establish that every measure would alter election results, that all described actions were implemented, or that a court had found the administration violated election law. The sourced account is therefore a report of CAP’s allegations and examples, with the legal and electoral effects left open.

terminal_record.title: DOJ Found Poor Judgment in Acosta's Epstein Non-Prosecution Agreement
terminal_record.description_short: The Epstein agreement was signed on September 24, 2007; DOJ later found Acosta used poor judgment, but no improper factors or professional misconduct.
terminal_record.description_medium: Jeffrey Epstein's federal non-prosecution agreement was signed on September 24, 2007, as a state-based resolution of the federal investigation. DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility later found that Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in choosing that resolution and in failing to ensure victims received notice, but said the decision fell within his discretion and was not based on improper factors. The reviewed report excerpt does not corroborate the original card's separate allegation of direct Trump pressure.
terminal_record.description_long: DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility documents that the federal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein was resolved through a non-prosecution agreement signed on September 24, 2007. The agreement ended the Southern District of Florida's federal investigation and forwent federal prosecution of Epstein, four named co-conspirators, and “any potential co-conspirators”; victims were not informed or consulted before signing. In 2020, OPR concluded that then-U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in resolving the case through the agreement and in failing to ensure that Florida would notify victims about the state plea hearing. OPR also said Acosta acted within his broad discretion, found no improper factors behind the decision, and did not find professional misconduct. This card keeps the documented agreement and review outcome while removing the unsupported assertion that Jeffrey Sloman documented direct political pressure from Donald Trump. The accessed DOJ report excerpt does not independently establish that Trump intervened, nor does it establish the opposite; that question remains outside this supported copy. The date follows the agreement's signing, not Epstein's June 2008 state-court plea.
organization_tags: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida

terminal_record.title: At the 2016 Debate, Trump Said He Would Cut Taxes “Big League”
terminal_record.description_short: The official transcript records Trump saying “big league,” not “bigly,” while discussing taxes and regulation at the September 2016 debate.
terminal_record.description_medium: At the September 26, 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, Trump argued about taxes and regulation. The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript records him saying, “I’m going to cut taxes big league,” and then saying Clinton would “raise taxes big league.” It does not record the word “bigly,” so this entry should use “big league” and avoid claims about audience reaction or Trump’s language ability that the transcript does not establish.
terminal_record.description_long: During the first 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, moderator Lester Holt moved the candidates through a discussion of prosperity and economic plans. In that exchange, Donald Trump criticized Hillary Clinton’s tax and regulatory proposals, then said: “I’m going to cut regulations. I’m going to cut taxes big league, and you’re going to raise taxes big league, end of story.” The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript therefore supports “big league” as the phrase used in this sentence. It does not support a claim that Trump said “bigly” here. This correction is narrow: it records the wording in the official transcript and does not decide what Trump intended, whether listeners misheard it, or how widely a later interpretation circulated. The packet offers no verified evidence for the old card’s claims that this phrase became a viral phenomenon or a measure of Trump’s vocabulary. Treat this as an accurately quoted debate remark, not as evidence of a policy, legal violation, or lasting public effect.

terminal_record.title: House Republicans Proposed Tightening Universal School-Meal Eligibility
terminal_record.description_short: A March 2025 House Republican budget proposal would raise the school-meal CEP threshold from 25% to 60%.
terminal_record.description_medium: Chalkbeat reported that a House Republican budget proposal would raise the Community Eligibility Provision threshold from 25% to 60%. An advocacy-group estimate cited in the report projected that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. The story describes a proposal, not an enacted March rollback.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 12, 2025, Chalkbeat reported that House Republicans were considering a budget proposal to make schools meet a stricter threshold before using the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), which lets qualifying schools serve meals at no charge to all enrolled students. At the time, the minimum identified-student percentage was 25 percent under USDA’s 2023 final rule. The proposal described in the report would raise the threshold to 60 percent. Chalkbeat attributed to an advocacy organization the estimate that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. Those figures were projected consequences of a proposal, not measured losses after an enacted rule. The sources reviewed do not establish that USDA completed a March 2025 cancellation of CEP, that 4 to 5 million children immediately lost meals, or that families experienced the harms stated in the frozen synopsis. This repaired entry therefore describes the threatened eligibility change and identifies Congress as the source of the proposal; it does not attribute a completed rollback to the Trump administration or state that the proposal itself became law.

source_fact_map.quote: The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: One proposal would dramatically increase the share of students who need to be enrolled in aid programs — such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families — for schools to be eligible to serve free meals to all kids through the Community Eligibility Provision. Right now, schools need to show 25% of students are enrolled in those kinds of assistance programs to participate in community eligibility. The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.

terminal_record.title: Trump Hosts Baltic Leaders and Reaffirms U.S. Partnership
terminal_record.description_short: Trump welcomed Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania’s leaders at an April 3, 2018 summit and publicly reaffirmed U.S. partnership.
terminal_record.description_medium: At a White House working lunch and U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit on April 3, 2018, President Trump welcomed the leaders of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. He congratulated the countries on their independence centennials and publicly affirmed a renewed partnership and U.S. recognition of their sovereignty. The original synopsis’s alleged private remark to aides that the leaders were “all the same” is not substantiated by this public transcript.
terminal_record.description_long: On April 3, 2018, President Donald Trump received the leaders of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania at the White House for a working lunch and the U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit. Trump congratulated the three countries on the 100th anniversary of their independence and said he was honored to host them. In his remarks, he said the United States had never ceased recognizing the sovereignty of the three Baltic republics and added, “we never let you down. And we won’t let you down.” He described the summit as renewing a partnership grounded in sovereignty and respect for the rule of law. His remarks also previewed discussions about bilateral trade, investment, and military-equipment purchases. The archived transcript supports this public meeting and the statements made there. It does not include the private “all the same” comment attributed to Trump in the original synopsis, and targeted searches did not corroborate that quotation. This narrowed record preserves the documented summit while removing the unsupported private allegation and the inference that it showed indifference to NATO commitments. The transcript does not record private conversations.

source_fact_map.fact: The archived transcript dates Trump's working-lunch remarks to April 3, 2018.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
Remarks by President Trump Before a Working Lunch with Heads of the Baltic States

Issued on: April 3, 2018

PRESIDENT TRUMP: Today, it’s my pleasure to congratulate Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania on the 100th anniversary of their independence. That’s really quite a great achievement, and congratulations. And I’m honored to have you with us in the White House and the Oval Office.

From the very beginning of your countries’ independence, the United States never — and this is, like, never — and I think you know that better than anybody — never ceased to recognize the sovereignty of the three Baltic republics, even though, throughout the years, there’s been a lot of conflict, a lot of problems, a lot of difficulty, and we never let you down. And we won’t let you down.

At today’s U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit, we’re inaugurating 100 years of renewed partnership among our nations, grounded once more in our shared commitment to independent sovereignty and a total respect of the rule of law.

terminal_record.description_short: USDA’s July 10 notice listed WIC among food programs treated as federal public benefits; it did not announce the frozen record’s claimed February nationwide ban.
terminal_record.description_medium: On July 10, 2025, USDA published a notice interpreting PRWORA’s federal-public-benefit definition and listing WIC among the Food and Nutrition Service’s programs. USDA said it was still evaluating how to verify compliance and would issue later guidance. The notice supports a July agency interpretation, not a February blanket exclusion of lawful immigrant families. A contemporaneous NILC analysis said states could choose whether to offer or restrict WIC; it reported Idaho was the only state restricting federally funded WIC that month.
terminal_record.description_long: On July 10, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture published a notice interpreting how the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act applies to the programs it administers. The notice included the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) among Food and Nutrition Service programs meeting the statute’s federal-public-benefit definition. USDA said it was still evaluating how to verify compliance and planned to issue later guidance. A contemporaneous National Immigration Law Center analysis said states could choose whether to offer or restrict WIC; it reported that Idaho alone had restricted federally funded WIC by July 2025. The notice documents a July federal interpretation, not a February nationwide ban on lawful immigrant families. The available sources do not establish an automatic cutoff for every WIC participant or document beneficiary-level outcomes. The notice did not state that every WIC recipient would be disqualified.

children.description_short: DOJ Memo Orders FBI Personnel Actions Tied to January 6 Cases
children.description_medium: Reuters reported that a January 31, 2025 memo ordered eight FBI officials to resign or be fired because of their work on January 6 cases. The bureau’s biography says Kash Patel did not become FBI director until February 20. The available reporting does not establish that all eight were ultimately dismissed or support attributing the January memo to Patel.
children.description_long: Reuters reported that a memo issued on January 31, 2025 ordered eight FBI officials to resign or be fired because of their participation in January 6 cases. Reuters also reported requests for employee lists tied to several investigations, but its accessible account names a 2024 Hamas-related prosecution and the two Trump cases brought by special counsel Jack Smith; it does not substantiate a separate claim that every January 6 investigator was included on a list. Patel did not direct this action as FBI director: the bureau’s biography states he became director on February 20, 2025. This child isolates the pre-confirmation personnel memo from later policies under Patel, including a headquarters-transfer plan and reported leak investigations. The available sources support the memo and its order concerning eight officials, but do not show that all eight were ultimately fired, the terms of their departures, or a final aggregate count of career staff removed. The original claim that Patel personally began a first-month purge of at least 75 officials is unsupported by these sources and is not carried into this child record.

children.title: FBI Managers Told Up to 1,500 Staff Would Move From Headquarters
children.description_short: FBI Managers Told Up to 1,500 Staff Would Move From Headquarters
children.description_medium: On February 21, 2025, The Washington Post reported that FBI managers were told up to 1,500 staff and agents would move from headquarters to field offices. The report described a planned transfer and a stated goal of bolstering field staffing; it did not establish that the plan was completed or intended to force resignations.
children.description_long: On February 21, 2025, The Washington Post reported that FBI managers had been told that up to 1,500 staff and agents would be transferred from the bureau’s Washington headquarters to field offices around the country. The article attributed the number and message to people briefed on the announcement, who spoke anonymously because it had not been publicly announced. The report placed the move in the context of Kash Patel’s newly confirmed leadership and said he had described bolstering field-office staffing as a priority. This supports a planned transfer and the stated rationale of shifting personnel toward field operations. It does not show that all 1,500 transfers occurred, that the FBI relocated its headquarters out of Washington, or that the plan was designed to force employees to resign. Those stronger claims appeared in the original combined entry without support in the cited report. This child keeps the transfer plan dated separately from pre-confirmation DOJ actions and later polygraph-based leak investigations. Its effects on individual employees and field-office staffing are unknown.

It also does not establish the number of examinations, the number of agencies involved, or any final disciplinary outcomes. This issue belongs in a separate record from January personnel directives made before Patel became FBI director and from the February headquarters-transfer plan. terminal_record.title: DOGE Lease List Targets 47 SSA Sites; SSA Says Most Were Unstaffed Hearing Rooms
terminal_record.description_short: AP reported 47 SSA locations on a lease-cancellation list, with 26 listed for 2025; SSA said most were unstaffed hearing rooms.
terminal_record.description_medium: AP reported March 19 that DOGE’s lease-cancellation list included 47 SSA locations, with 26 expected to close during 2025. On March 27, SSA said no local field office had been permanently closed or announced for closure since January 1, and said most listed sites were unstaffed hearing rooms. The record supports a planned lease action, not the original claim that 600 field offices closed or a documented loss of service.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 19, 2025, the Associated Press reported that DOGE had listed 47 Social Security Administration offices for lease cancellation and that 26 entries were expected to close during the year, based on General Services Administration data. This was a plan tied to lease terminations, not proof that 47 public field offices had permanently closed. SSA responded on March 27 that no local field office had been permanently closed or announced for permanent closure since January 1. The agency said most sites identified to GSA were small hearing rooms without assigned employees; it separately said it had announced closure of one hearing office in White Plains, New York. The available records support a proposed lease-termination effort at SSA locations, with facility types and dates varying across the list. They do not support the original claim that about 600 of roughly 1,200 field offices were closed. The sources reviewed also do not establish that every lease cancellation occurred or quantify resulting service loss, delays, or harm to claimants. This entry records the plan and the agency’s contemporaneous correction; outcomes at individual locations remain uncertain.

terminal_record.title: 1993 Mar-a-Lago Use Agreement Prohibited Membership Discrimination
terminal_record.description_short: A 1993 Palm Beach agreement governing Mar-a-Lago's club use barred discrimination against prospective members on listed grounds.
terminal_record.description_medium: On August 10, 1993, Donald Trump, Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc., and the Town of Palm Beach entered a Declaration of Use Agreement governing the property’s private-club use. The agreement prohibited discrimination against prospective members on enumerated grounds, including race and religion. The document supports a 1993 membership rule; it does not establish a 2013 discrimination lawsuit or settlement, or prove how the rule was enforced.
terminal_record.description_long: On August 10, 1993, Donald J. Trump, the Town of Palm Beach, and The Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc. entered a Declaration of Use Agreement as the property was approved for use as a private social club. The recorded agreement says the Club “shall not discriminate against any prospective member” on listed grounds that include race, color, and religion. It set a nondiscrimination condition for prospective club membership. The document does not report a finding that Mar-a-Lago had discriminated, identify a plaintiff harmed by discrimination, or describe a 2013 lawsuit. PolitiFact’s review of a related but distinct Palm Beach dispute says Trump sued the town in 1996, alleging the town discriminated against Mar-a-Lago because it admitted Jewish and African American members; the town disputed that allegation. That was a claim by Trump against the town, not a case against the club brought by residents. This entry replaces the unsupported 2013-settlement story with the specific contractual clause established by the 1993 agreement. It does not infer whether the clause was enforced or whether it changed the club’s actual membership practices.

held_record.title: Trump Claims Census Report Shows Noncitizens Voted in 2020 Election
held_record.synopsis: President Donald Trump has cited a census report as evidence that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. However, experts have questioned the validity of the analysis, raising concerns about the potential spread of misinformation and the impact on election integrity.

survivor_record.title: Trump Claims Census Report Shows Noncitizens Voted in 2020 Election
survivor_record.synopsis: President Donald Trump has claimed that a census report shows 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. However, experts have questioned the analysis and validity of the report.
survivor_record.description_medium: On August 20, 2026, Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming that about 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election and said it supported his claim that he won. Votebeat reported that election experts questioned the analysis because it omitted authors, detailed methods, and a margin of error. The outlet said the number, even if accurate, would not have changed the result. The Census Bureau did not respond to its request for comment.
survivor_record.description_long: On August 20, 2026, President Donald Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis that claimed, with high confidence, that approximately 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 presidential election. He said the result supported his repeated assertion that he had won that election. Votebeat reported that experts questioned the study's reliability because it did not identify its authors, explain the data's reliability in detail, or provide a margin of error. The analysis reportedly matched voter files with federal immigration records, and the data provider said it was surprised to see its files used for this purpose. The reported 24,000 figure represented less than 0.019% of the more than 128 million voters examined. Votebeat noted that even if the number were accurate, it was too small to change the outcome; it also said the analysis could not determine whether those voters supported Trump or Joe Biden. The Census Bureau did not respond to the outlet's request for comment. These distinctions matter: the report describes a government analysis and a presidential claim, alongside expert concerns about methodology. It does not establish that noncitizen voting affected the 2020 result.

children.description_short: Trump issues Proclamation 10886 declaring a national emergency at the southern border.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued Proclamation 10886, declaring a national emergency at the southern border. children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10886, “Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern Border of the United States.” The proclamation’s opening presents the administration’s view that the border faced an invasion and describes harms it attributed to unlawful migration, cartels and narcotics. Those are the President’s claims in the proclamation, not independent findings established by the document’s publication. The proclamation directs executive agencies to take actions using specified authorities and resources. It is distinct from the March 15 proclamation that invoked the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals the administration alleged were members of Tren de Aragua. The January declaration did not itself invoke that Act. This record captures the emergency declaration and its stated basis without claiming that the declaration began a mass-deportation program, establishing the truth of every factual assertion in its preamble, or adding later enforcement outcomes.

children.description_long: On March 15, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act in relation to Tren de Aragua. The proclamation asserts that the group was perpetrating or threatening an invasion or predatory incursion and declares certain Venezuelan citizens alleged to be members liable to apprehension, restraint, detention and removal, subject to the criteria it sets out. It directs the Attorney General and the Homeland Security secretary to carry out those measures. The group-membership and invasion statements are the administration’s assertions in the proclamation, not findings by a court that the allegations about each person are true. This action is distinct from the January 20 border emergency proclamation; it occurred nearly two months later and expressly invokes the Alien Enemies Act. This entry describes the issuance and the removal directive without claiming that every person covered was removed or that legal challenges resolved the policy’s validity.

terminal_record.title: Trump's January 19, 2021 Clemency List Included Drug-Conviction Commutations
terminal_record.description_short: DOJ's January 19, 2021 commutations roster includes recipients with federal cocaine and methamphetamine convictions.
terminal_record.description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted commutations to multiple people whose convictions involved federal drug offenses. The Justice Department's archived commutations roster lists recipients by clemency date and identifies offenses, including cocaine-distribution conspiracy and methamphetamine-manufacture conspiracy. The roster does not report petition histories, lobbying, payments, or a rationale for each grant.
terminal_record.description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted clemency to a group of recipients whose DOJ roster entries include federal drug convictions. The archived Office of the Pardon Attorney commutations list places recipients under that date and identifies their districts, sentences, and offenses. For example, the list records David Morris Barren's cocaine-distribution conspiracy conviction and Kristina Kay Bohnenkamp's methamphetamine-manufacture conspiracy conviction. This narrower account preserves the documented drug-related clemency activity from the original card without asserting that recipients had never submitted petitions or that money secured their grants. The DOJ roster does not publish recipient-level petition histories or identify paid intermediaries. Legal commentary and contemporaneous reporting reviewed for this repair describe petition bypasses and paid clemency lobbying in other cases, but the material accessed does not connect payments to these named recipients or show an exchange for clemency. No count beyond the two examples is claimed here, and the entry does not attribute a motive to Trump. The original card's broader allegations are excluded.

terminal_record.title: Internal Draft: Supplied April 2025 Pell-Restriction Claim Remains Unverified
terminal_record.description_short: Internal Draft: Supplied April 2025 Pell-Restriction Claim Remains Unverified
terminal_record.description_medium: The supplied record alleges that an April 2025 rule removed Pell access for several groups, but no contemporaneous rule or source is included. The accessed Education Department pages describe a July 2025 interpretation and a later Workforce Pell expansion; they do not verify the alleged April cutoff. This remains an internal, unverified draft with the original claims treated as allegations.
terminal_record.description_long: This internal draft records the supplied allegation that, in April 2025, the administration restricted Pell eligibility for undocumented students, short-term credential learners, and students at institutions cited under new anti-DEI rules. The packet contains no April rule text, contemporaneous notice, or source linking those groups to one action, so the allegation remains unverified. The accessible Education Department release is dated July 2025: it describes an interpretive rule affecting eligibility verification for certain career, technical, and adult-education benefits, and says Pell Grants and federal student loans remained unavailable to people who did not qualify under existing rules. The Department said its interpretive rule was not binding; the accessed page also records a later court-related stay of potential enforcement through September 10, 2025. A separate Workforce Pell announcement says qualifying short-term programs could receive Pell funding beginning July 1, 2026, which does not support an April 2025 elimination of short-term Pell. The supplied claims about anti-DEI institution exclusions, reduced award amounts, and projected impacts on students are not established by these pages and are not presented as findings. The April date, covered populations, legal mechanism, and consequences remain unknown. Keep this draft internal until an April rule or reliable contemporaneous reporting is available.
terminal_record.date_start_basis: Date supplied in the frozen record; no accessed source confirms an April rule or action.

terminal_record.title: June Report Describes FBI Personnel Actions Against Senior Agents
terminal_record.description_short: June 2025 reporting described FBI personnel actions involving senior agents and a top deputy.
terminal_record.description_medium: Reporting dated June 5, 2025 described FBI leadership forcing two veteran agents out and disciplining a third employee. The New York Times named Spencer Evans, Stanley Meador and Michael Feinberg; its account attributed details to people familiar with the matter. The reporting supports a narrow FBI personnel episode, not the frozen claim that Defense and Intelligence Community inspectors general were fired in June.
terminal_record.description_long: The New York Times reported on June 5, 2025, that the FBI targeted several employees in personnel actions. Its article said two veteran agents in Virginia were forced out and another employee in Las Vegas was punished, citing people familiar with the matter. The report named Spencer Evans and Stanley Meador as senior agents who ran field offices in Las Vegas and Richmond, and Michael Feinberg as a top deputy in Norfolk. The article’s summary says an agent threatened with demotion opted to resign while two others were forced to move and retire; it does not identify each consequence with each named person in the excerpts accessed here. The Times placed the episode among transfers, ousters and demotions as Kash Patel reshaped the bureau. It reported that current and former agents characterized the broader changes as retaliation; that is an attributed view, not a legal finding. The available reporting supports a narrow June FBI personnel account. It does not support the frozen record’s claims that Defense or Intelligence Community inspectors general were removed or that these actions eliminated the last internal checks. The January inspector-general report previously linked to the record concerns a separate event.

terminal_record.title: Iran Nuclear Talks Had No Resumption Date as of July 14, 2025
terminal_record.description_short: Iranian officials said July 14, 2025, that no date or location had been set to resume U.S.-Iran nuclear talks after the June conflict.
terminal_record.description_medium: On July 14, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said no date or location had been set for resumed U.S.-Iran nuclear talks when asked about a possible meeting between Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Reuters had reported on July 1 that G7 foreign ministers urged negotiations to resume after the Iran-Israel ceasefire. These reports support an unscheduled diplomatic process, not Trump’s repeated promise of an imminent “historic, perfect” deal or a definitive collapse by July’s end.

The status followed the June ceasefire between Israel and Iran. On July 1, Reuters reported that Group of Seven foreign ministers had urged negotiations to resume for an agreement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. The same Reuters report said the United States and Iran had held talks since April and quoted Witkoff describing them as “promising,” while Washington hoped for a long-term peace deal. These sources trace the diplomatic context but do not establish that Trump repeatedly promised in July that a “historic, perfect” agreement was imminent. Nor do they show negotiations completely collapsed by July 31. The supported event is narrower: talks were unscheduled as of July 14 after a June conflict and a G7 appeal to resume negotiations. This evidence does not establish that a particular public statement damaged U.S. credibility, and the frozen entry’s causal judgment is not carried into this corrected copy. The reporting also does not establish that Iranian officials denied all serious talks were taking place.

terminal_record.title: Trump Claims an “Absolute Right” to Pardon Himself
terminal_record.description_short: In a June 4, 2018 tweet, Trump claimed an absolute right to pardon himself during the Mueller investigation; he did not issue a self-pardon.
terminal_record.description_medium: On June 4, 2018, President Donald Trump tweeted that he had the “absolute right” to pardon himself while discussing the special counsel’s Russia investigation. He said he would not do so because he had done nothing wrong. This was a claim about presidential authority, not an issued pardon; the cited reporting describes the constitutional question as disputed.
terminal_record.description_long: On June 4, 2018, while Robert Mueller’s investigation was underway, President Donald Trump publicly claimed that he had an “absolute right” to pardon himself. In the same tweet, he said he had done nothing wrong and asked why he would use such a pardon. Associated Press coverage described the statement as asserting presidential power during the administration’s legal defense against the Russia investigation. Trump did not issue a self-pardon in the reported statement, and the sources do not show an order purporting to pardon him. The claim concerned whether a president could exercise the constitutional pardon power over himself; the question was disputed and no court ruling in this record resolves it. This corrected card dates the statement to June 2018. It does not attribute a self-pardon announcement to Trump’s return to office in January 2025, and it does not say that the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling conferred a pardon power. It records the public assertion and preserves the difference between an argument about authority and an act using that authority.

impact_proposal.rationale: The verified event is a president's public claim of self-pardon authority during an active federal investigation. No pardon was issued in the cited account, so this proposal scores no realized harm or private benefit and only limited institutional pressure.

terminal_record.title: HUD Terminates Fair-Housing Grants; Evidence Does Not Show an Office-Wide Shutdown
terminal_record.description_short: A court filing describes HUD's immediate termination of 78 FHIP grants in February 2025, not a shutdown of all fair-housing enforcement.
terminal_record.description_medium: A March 13, 2025 federal court filing describes HUD notices terminating 78 active Fair Housing Initiatives Program grants effective February 27. The filing quotes the notices’ stated reason and says no further explanation was provided. This supports a targeted grant action affecting nonprofit fair-housing work. The sources reviewed do not establish that HUD ended every proactive investigation, zeroed out FHEO’s budget, or disabled all federal enforcement.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 27, 2025, the Department of Housing and Urban Development terminated 78 active Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP) grants. A March 13 federal court filing by fair-housing organizations describes form notices making the terminations effective immediately and quotes the notice as saying the awards no longer effectuated program goals or agency priorities. The filing says the notices attributed the decision to presidential direction under the order establishing the Department of Government Efficiency. Those statements document the notices as quoted in the plaintiffs’ filing; the filing is not a judicial finding that the action was unlawful. The supported scope is the specified FHIP awards and their nonprofit recipients. The evidence reviewed does not establish that HUD ended all proactive fair-housing investigations, zeroed out the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity budget, or stopped every form of federal enforcement. Claims about staffing reductions and downstream service losses require their own evidence and are not asserted here. The card therefore records the narrower documented grant action, distinguishes the court challenge from a court ruling, and leaves the broader office-wide claims unresolved.

terminal_record.title: Trump’s FY2026 Budget Proposed Replacing Housing Choice Vouchers With State Grants
terminal_record.description_short: The FY2026 budget proposed replacing federal voucher-account funding with state rental assistance; Congress later funded Housing Choice Vouchers for 2026.
terminal_record.description_medium: HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget justification, available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance, which includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the state grant as intended to replace federal rental-assistance programs. This was a budget proposal, not an April 2025 cancellation of new vouchers; Congress enacted 2026 voucher funding on February 3, 2026.
terminal_record.description_long:
HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget request, made available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance (TBRA), the federal account that includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new state-run State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the design as eliminating federal rental-assistance programs, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, and replacing them with a state block grant. HUD’s budget materials describe TBRA as the account serving about 2.3 million families in 2025.

This supports a corrected entry about a proposed federal funding redesign, not the frozen claim that the administration announced an April 2025 stop to new vouchers. The budget materials do not show that applicants were removed from waiting lists, existing vouchers were rescinded, homelessness increased, or tens of thousands of households lost assistance; those consequences should not be asserted here. Nor was the proposal enacted as a voucher shutdown: HUD later reported that the Consolidated Appropriations Act signed February 3, 2026 provided funding for the Housing Choice Voucher program. Keep the entry centered on what the administration proposed, distinguish the proposal from the later enacted funding, and leave actual household effects unclaimed.

terminal_record.title: Trump Pardoned Three Former Border Patrol Agents in December 2020
terminal_record.description_short: Trump pardoned former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos, Jose Compean and Gary Brugman in December 2020.
terminal_record.description_medium: Trump pardoned Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and Gary Brugman on December 23. The White House and Texas Tribune sources describe their separate convictions involving assault or deprivation of civil rights. The January 2025 clemency proclamation concerned January 6-related offenses, so the original date is corrected to the documented 2020 actions.
terminal_record.description_long: President Donald Trump granted full pardons to former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and former agent Gary Brugman on December 23. The archived White House statement about Ramos and Compean says they were convicted of assault, a firearm offense and deprivation of civil rights in connection with the 2005 shooting of a man near the U.S.-Mexico border. A Texas Tribune report describes Brugman’s 2002 conviction for deprivation of rights after he struck detained migrants; the report says he served more than two years in federal prison. These grants occurred in December 2020, not as part of Trump’s January 20, 2025 clemency proclamation. The Justice Department describes that later proclamation as covering offenses relating to the January 6, 2021 Capitol events. This correction preserves the earlier pardons and the documented conviction records while removing the unsupported claim that the agents were pardoned in January 2025 or that all cited cases were the same event. It does not infer why Trump granted clemency or state that the convictions were later vacated.

terminal_record.title: DHS Ends Afghanistan’s TPS Designation Effective July 14, 2025
terminal_record.description_short: DHS terminated Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025.
terminal_record.description_medium: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14. The notice estimates about 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality last resident in Afghanistan held TPS; it separately notes about 3,600 were also approved lawful permanent residents. The sourced action concerns Afghanistan only and does not establish deportations or simultaneous TPS terminations for other nationalities.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s designation for Temporary Protected Status (TPS). The notice says the Secretary reviewed country conditions, consulted other U.S. agencies, and determined that Afghanistan no longer met the statutory conditions for TPS. The designation ended effective at 11:59 p.m. local time on July 14, 2025. DHS estimated approximately 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality who last habitually resided in Afghanistan held TPS under that designation. The notice also states that approximately 3,600 of that group had already been approved as lawful permanent residents. This entry is narrowed to the Afghanistan designation; it does not claim that Ukraine, Venezuela, Haiti, El Salvador, or other designations ended in the same March action. The notice establishes a change in legal status, not that former TPS holders were deported, returned to danger, or all lacked another immigration status. Those individual outcomes and the legal merits of the Secretary’s assessment are outside the evidence used here.
